response: Named Entity Recognition (NER) – the task of identifying and classifying named entities in text – is a fundamental component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including information extraction, question answering, and knowledge base construction (Nadeau & Sekine, 2007). Traditionally, NER systems heavily relied on hand-crafted features derived from linguistic knowledge and domain expertise (Ratinov & Roth, 2009; Chiang & Lin, 2007). However, the advent of deep learning techniques has led to substantial progress in NER, enabling the development of powerful systems that automatically learn feature representations from raw text (Huang et al., 2015; Ma & Hovy, 2016; Lample et al., 2016). Despite these advances, deep learning models typically require large amounts of manually annotated training data to achieve optimal performance. Annotating data is expensive and time-consuming, particularly for specialized domains where expert knowledge is often needed. This limitation has spurred research into alternative approaches that can leverage readily available, albeit less expensive, resources. Distant supervision, a paradigm that automatically generates training labels by aligning text with existing knowledge bases (KB) or dictionaries, has emerged as a promising solution (Mintz et al., 2009; Hakkani-Tür et al., 2010). In the context of NER, this often involves mapping entity mentions in text to corresponding entries in a dictionary. However, applying distant supervision is not without its challenges. The automatic labeling process is inherently noisy, as a single entity mention can correspond to multiple possible entity types, or even be incorrectly linked to an entity in the dictionary. Furthermore, dictionaries are often incomplete and may not cover all entity variations present in the text. Existing approaches to mitigate the effect of noisy labels have typically focused on incorporating more sophisticated learning algorithms (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017) or employing techniques such as multi-instance learning (Yao et al., 2017). While these methods can improve performance, they often require careful tuning and can still struggle in scenarios with high levels of noise. In this paper, we address the problem of learning effective NER models from noisy data generated through distant supervision. We propose two novel neural models specifically designed to handle the challenges of distant supervision using domain-specific dictionaries. First, within the standard sequence labeling framework, we introduce a revised Fuzzy CRF layer that effectively manages tokens with multiple potential labels. Recognizing the inherent limitations of this traditional approach, we then present a more radical departure: AutoNER, a novel neural model built upon a “Tie or Break” scheme that actively learns to either confidently assign a label based on dictionary evidence or defer to other contextual cues. Furthermore, we investigate techniques for refining the distant supervision process itself, aiming to create higher-quality training data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets. Our results show that AutoNER achieves state-of-the-art performance when trained solely using dictionaries, surpassing existing methods and even delivering competitive results compared to systems trained with considerably more human annotation.

Instead, evidence from both behavioral experiments (e.g., Rayner, 1998) and neuroimaging studies (e.g., Hagoort et al., 2003) suggests that we actively build syntactic structures and associated interpretations in a left-to-right, word-by-word fashion. response: Vector space models have long been a cornerstone of natural language processing, providing a powerful means of representing text as numerical vectors amenable to machine learning algorithms. Recent years have witnessed a surge in the popularity of distributional representations - dense, low-dimensional vectors trained to capture semantic relationships between words and phrases. These representations, such as word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of NLP tasks. Extending this success to the document level has been a primary focus, leading to the development of document embedding techniques like Doc2Vec (Le & Mikolov, 2014) and Paragraph Vectors (Mikolov et al., 2013). These models learn a fixed-length vector representation for each document, capturing its overall semantic meaning. However, existing document vector approaches often fall short when dealing with complex, multi-topic documents. Standard paragraph vector models tend to represent a document with a single, averaged vector, potentially losing nuanced topic information and failing to capture the diverse semantic contexts present within the text. Furthermore, these dense vector representations can be computationally expensive, both in terms of training time and memory requirements, hindering scalability for large datasets. Recent attempts to address these limitations, such as the Non-negative Tensor Singular Decomposition (NTSG) model (Liu et al., 2015a), have shown promising results but still face challenges in balancing performance with computational efficiency and the accurate representation of multifaceted documents. In this paper, we introduce Sparse Composite Document Vectors (SCDV), a novel feature vector formation technique designed to overcome the limitations of current document embedding methods. SCDV leverages the strengths of distributional word embeddings while incorporating a soft clustering mechanism to model multiple semantic contexts within a document. Critically, rather than averaging word embeddings or employing complex tensor decompositions, SCDV clusters word embeddings into semantic groups and then chains these groups together to form document-level topic vectors. This composite structure allows for a more nuanced representation of documents with diverse thematic content. Through extensive experimentation on both multi-class and multi-label classification tasks, we demonstrate that SCDV consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art NTSG model. Moreover, we showcase SCDV’s strong generalization capabilities across heterogeneous tasks including Topic Coherence evaluation, context-sensitive learning scenarios and Information Retrieval tasks. Notably, SCDV achieves significant reductions in both training and prediction times compared to existing methods, offering a compelling balance between performance and computational efficiency. In essence, SCDV provides a practical and effective solution for generating high-quality document embeddings that are both semantically rich and computationally tractable. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work in document embedding and dimensionality reduction techniques. Section 3 details the SCDV model and the underlying methodology. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses future research directions.

response: Bilingual Named Entity (NE) alignment – the task of identifying corresponding NEs in two different languages – is a critical component in various Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including machine translation, cross-lingual information retrieval, and multilingual knowledge base construction. Accurate NE alignment facilitates better understanding of multilingual documents, improves translation quality by ensuring consistent handling of proper nouns, and enables seamless integration of information extracted from diverse linguistic sources. Despite significant progress in NE recognition and machine translation, the task of *aligning* NEs across languages remains challenging. Existing methods often treat NE recognition and alignment as separate steps, leading to error propagation and suboptimal performance. For instance, a noisy NE recognizer can generate many false positives, which are then passed on to the alignment stage, increasing the search space and lowering alignment accuracy. Furthermore, the inherent ambiguity in NE translation poses a significant hurdle. Named entities can be translated in multiple ways – sometimes semantically equivalent terms are used (e.g., “New York” – “纽约”), while other times phonetic transliteration occurs (e.g., “Google” – “谷歌”), and in some instances, a combination of both or even descriptive paraphrases are employed. Traditional alignment approaches often struggle to account for this diversity and rely heavily on string matching or statistical co-occurrence, which can be unreliable when dealing with varying translation strategies. Recent work has explored more sophisticated alignment strategies, including utilizing parallel corpora and leveraging contextual information. However, these methods rarely capitalize on the strong relationship between NE type and translation behavior. Specifically, the way an NE is translated—whether it's literal translation, transliteration, or a descriptive equivalent—is heavily dependent on its entity type (PER, ORG, LOC, etc.). For example, organizations are frequently transliterated, while locations are more often translated semantically. Moreover, a fundamental assumption of accurate alignment is that NEs in a correctly aligned pair should share the same semantic type; one would not expect to align a person’s name with a location. In this paper, we leverage these observations to propose a novel integrated model for jointly recognizing and aligning bilingual NEs between Chinese and English. Our approach moves beyond treating these tasks as separate pipeline stages and instead frames them as a unified inference problem. We introduce a new feature, the “mapping type ratio,” which quantifies the proportion of internal tokens within an NE that undergo semantic translation – providing valuable evidence about the likely translation strategy. Additionally, we explicitly enforce an entity type consistency constraint during alignment, ensuring that aligned NEs possess the same type. Finally, we incorporate monolingual candidate certainty factors, derived from confidently recognized NEs (acting as anchors), to guide the alignment process and improve accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that our approach substantially improves the type-sensitive F-score for identified NE pairs, achieving a significant reduction in alignment error compared to previous methods. This work not only advances the state-of-the-art in bilingual NE alignment but also provides valuable insights into the interplay between NE recognition, type information, and translation strategies.

Unlike languages that explicitly delineate word boundaries with spaces, Chinese relies on identifying word segments within a continuous stream of characters. Traditional approaches to CWS involved dictionary-based methods, rule-based systems, and statistical models like Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) (Xue and Shen, 2003;Zhang and Lee, 2003). Further, acquiring large, accurately labeled datasets for CWS is both expensive and time-consuming. This limitation motivates research into methods for leveraging unlabeled data and semi-supervised learning techniques. One promising avenue for improving CWS performance is to employ character embeddings. Character embeddings represent each character as a dense vector, enabling models to generalize to unseen words and capture morphological similarities. Existing approaches often train character embeddings directly on the labeled CWS data, or utilize pre-trained embeddings from large text corpora. However, these methods may not fully exploit the potential of contextual information. Traditional Information Extraction (IE) systems, while successful in specific domains, rely heavily on manually defined patterns, ontologies, and supervised learning approaches – a process both costly and brittle when faced with the ever-expanding breadth of topics and linguistic variations on the web. Open Information Extraction (Open IE) emerged as a compelling alternative, aiming to automatically discover relations and entities directly from text *without* prior knowledge or domain-specific resources (Banko et al., 2008; Etzioni et al., 2008). This paradigm shift allows for greater scalability and adaptability, making Open IE particularly well-suited for analyzing the vast and heterogeneous content of the web. These approaches vary considerably in their underlying linguistic analyses, relation extraction techniques, and overall system architectures. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the evolution of Open IE, detailing the key methods developed to date. Our discussion begins with an outline of the core challenges inherent in Open IE, including relation ambiguity, the lack of predefined schemas, and the need for robust handling of linguistic variation. We then trace the development of Open IE techniques chronologically, categorizing them into distinct phases reflecting major shifts in methodology. Early approaches primarily focused on pattern-based extraction, leveraging syntactic parses and heuristics to identify relational triples. Subsequent work explored unsupervised learning techniques, employing clustering and distributional semantics to discover relations without labeled data. More recently, research has incorporated neural network models, leveraging their ability to learn complex patterns and represent semantic information. Furthermore, we critically assess the dominant evaluation methodologies used in Open IE research. response: The ability to identify paraphrases – different ways of expressing the same information need – is a core task in natural language processing (NLP) with broad applications. These range from improving information retrieval (IR) systems by expanding queries to enhancing the performance of question answering (QA) and machine translation (MT) systems. Traditional approaches to paraphrase identification have often relied on manually constructed datasets, lexical resources like WordNet, or sophisticated semantic analysis techniques. However, these methods can be expensive to develop and maintain, and may not generalize well to novel contexts or domains. More recently, researchers have begun to leverage the vast quantities of data available in search engine logs as a source of paraphrase information. Search logs implicitly contain numerous paraphrases, as users frequently refine their initial queries with alternative formulations in an attempt to find more relevant results. A user's iterative query reformulations within a search session often represent attempts to express the same underlying information need using different wording. However, not all query pairs within a search session constitute true paraphrases. Many pairs may express related, but distinct, information needs, or simply represent navigational queries. This presents a significant challenge: how to accurately distinguish between genuine paraphrases and simply related queries within search log data. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a novel approach that incorporates user behavior information gleaned from search log sessions. We hypothesize that the ways in which users interact with search results – specifically, their clicking patterns and dwell times – can provide valuable clues as to whether two queries represent the same underlying information need. For instance, if a user submits two queries and clicks on the same set of results for both, this strongly suggests that the queries are paraphrases. Conversely, if a user clicks on different sets of results, it is more likely that the queries represent distinct information needs. We formulate the problem of paraphrase pattern learning as a classification task. Alongside conventional features such as lexical similarity and query length, we introduce three novel types of features that capture user behavior: click overlap, session position, and dwell time. These features, derived from analysis of query sessions, allow our model to better discriminate between true paraphrases and related queries. We evaluate our method using a large-scale query log from a commercial search engine. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, and crucially, highlight the significant contribution of the user behavior features to improved paraphrase identification. We are able to extract over 250,000 high-precision (over 76%) paraphrase patterns from the search log data, demonstrating the practical utility of our method. In essence, we argue that user behaviors lend a helping hand in deciphering the often-subtle nuances of language expressed within search log sessions, allowing us to unlock a rich source of paraphrase knowledge for a variety of NLP applications. We believe this is a valuable step toward building more robust and adaptable paraphrase identification systems. . . . . . . . . . . . . .

While they might appear in superficially similar contexts – for example, describing reactions to events – their emotional connotations are diametrically opposed. Consequently, standard word embeddings may inadvertently place “happy” and “sad” closer together in vector space than “happy” and “joy,” a clear semantic and affective mismatch. Accurate morphological segmentation is crucial for a variety of downstream tasks, including machine translation, information retrieval, and speech recognition, particularly for morphologically rich languages. Traditionally, morphological segmentation has relied heavily on manually annotated data, which is costly and time-consuming to create, and often unavailable for low-resource languages. Consequently, there’s been growing interest in unsupervised and semi-supervised methods capable of learning morphological structure from raw text. Morfessor (Creutz and Lagus, 2007) is a family of well-established methods designed for unsupervised morphological segmentation. It operates on the principle of Maximum Entropy Markov Models (MEMMs) and has proven effective across a range of languages. Existing Morfessor variants, such as Baseline and Categories-MAP, have achieved strong performance, becoming established baselines in the field. However, these methods can be computationally intensive, and the underlying MEMM framework presents certain limitations in terms of model expressiveness and ease of extension. In this paper, we introduce FlatCat, a novel variant of Morfessor that adopts a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) framework. FlatCat builds upon the foundational components of previous Morfessor models, inheriting the familiar morphotactic and morpheme-selection stages. However, by recasting the segmentation process within an HMM structure, we aim to gain benefits in terms of computational efficiency, model interpretability, and the potential for incorporating richer linguistic information. The HMM formulation allows for a more principled probabilistic treatment of segmentation ambiguity, leading to more robust and accurate results. Our experiments demonstrate that FlatCat, in its unsupervised configuration, achieves performance comparable to, though slightly below, the established Categories-MAP variant. However, the true strength of FlatCat emerges in the semi-supervised setting. response: Relation extraction (RE) – the task of identifying semantic relationships between entities mentioned in text – is a cornerstone of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including knowledge base completion (KB completion), question answering, and information retrieval (Etzioni et al., 2008;Popescu et al., 2003;Banko et al., 2007). Traditionally, RE systems have relied on either manually crafted rules (Hsu and Chu-Ren Wang, 2008) or supervised machine learning methods trained on annotated data (Zheng et al., 2017;Miwa and Bansal, 2016). However, manual rule creation is time-consuming and lacks scalability, while supervised learning demands substantial labeled data, a costly and bottlenecking requirement. More recently, a paradigm shift towards distant supervision and pattern-based methods has gained prominence (Mintz et al., 2009;Spoerri et al., 2008). Distant supervision automatically generates training instances by aligning text with existing knowledge bases (KBs), enabling learning without manual annotation. Pattern-based methods, on the other hand, directly extract relations by identifying textual patterns that reliably indicate specific relationships. These patterns often take the form of lexical or syntactic structures surrounding entity pairs. A key challenge within this approach is identifying robust and accurate patterns that generalize well across different contexts. Despite advancements in pattern-based RE, existing resources often suffer from limitations. Many pattern collections are relatively small, domain-specific, or lack semantic organization. Furthermore, evaluating the quality and relationships between patterns remains a significant hurdle. Existing work mostly focuses on identifying patterns for a limited set of relations, and a comprehensive, semantically structured taxonomy of relational patterns is lacking. To address these limitations, we introduce PATTY (Pattern Taxonomy with Typed Yields): a large-scale resource for textual patterns denoting binary relations between entities. PATTY goes beyond simple pattern enumeration; it provides a semantically typed and organized taxonomy of these patterns, leveraging the rich type information from large knowledge bases and efficient algorithms for pattern discovery. Built on the principles of frequent itemset mining applied to web-scale corpora, PATTY effectively captures commonly observed patterns while ensuring a high degree of accuracy. The core contribution of this work is the creation of a comprehensive and organized resource of relational patterns. PATTY contains 350,569 pattern synsets, arranged into a taxonomy with 8,162 subsumption relationships. We present a rigorous evaluation demonstrating that PATTY achieves a pattern accuracy of 84.7% and a subsumption precision of 75%, confirming its reliability and organization. Furthermore, we are making PATTY publicly available to promote further research in relation extraction and related NLP tasks. Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) represent a rich, yet largely untapped, source of information for a wide range of applications, including clinical decision support, patient risk stratification, and population health management. However, effectively harnessing the information contained within EMRs requires overcoming substantial challenges, primarily stemming from the complex and often unstructured nature of clinical notes, as well as the need for specialized knowledge to interpret medical terminology and context. Question Answering (QA) offers a particularly promising avenue for accessing and utilizing this information, enabling clinicians and researchers to pose natural language queries and receive concise, evidence-based answers directly from patient records. In this paper, we present emrQA, a novel large-scale QA dataset for electronic medical records, generated through a resourceful methodology: re-purposing existing annotations from established NLP tasks. Rather than embarking on a costly new annotation project, we leverage the wealth of expert annotations already available within the i2b2 shared task datasets (Uzuner et al., 2007; Denny et al., 2013; Stark et al., 2016). Understanding ‘who did what to whom, when, where, and why’ is crucial for deeper semantic interpretation and downstream applications such as question answering, information extraction, and machine translation (Dorr et al., 2007;Màrquez et al., 2008;Kipper et al., 2009). Traditionally, SRL systems heavily relied on rich linguistic features, particularly those derived from syntactic parsing (Gildea and Jurafsky, 2002;Màrquez et al., 2008). The intuition behind this reliance is that syntactic structure provides valuable cues for identifying semantic roles: arguments often occupy specific syntactic positions relative to the predicate. For example, the subject of a verb is frequently the nominal constituent immediately to the left of the verb in a dependency parse. Indeed, initial successes in SRL were often predicated on high-quality syntactic parsers and meticulously engineered features capturing syntactic relationships (Palmer et al., 2005). These features included dependency path lengths, voice (active/passive), and subtree patterns. However, the rise of deep learning has fundamentally altered the landscape of SRL. Recent neural network-based models (Zhou et al., 2016;He et al., 2017;Tan et al., 2018) have demonstrated impressive performance, often surpassing previous state-of-the-art systems *without* explicitly incorporating a syntactic backbone. These models learn representations directly from raw text, leveraging the power of distributed representations and complex non-linear transformations. At the heart of these systems lie bilingual lexicons – dictionaries mapping words and phrases between two languages. Traditionally, the construction of such lexicons has been a laborious, time-consuming, and expensive undertaking, requiring the expertise of skilled bilingual lexicographers. While massively parallel corpora and statistical machine translation methods have lessened the dependence on manually curated lexicons to some extent, they haven't rendered them obsolete. Indeed, specialized domains often require tailored lexicons that capture the nuances of terminology not adequately represented in general-purpose resources. Several automatic methods have been proposed to circumvent the limitations of manual lexicon construction. These methods typically leverage comparable corpora – collections of texts in different languages covering the same subject matter – and employ techniques like statistical alignment or cross-lingual document classification to identify plausible translation pairs. However, many of these approaches are constrained by data sparsity, particularly for low-resource languages, and rely on the availability of sizable comparable corpora, a resource not readily available for all language pairs or specialized domains. Furthermore, the performance of these automatically generated lexicons often falls significantly short of that of manually crafted resources, hindering the overall quality of MT and CLIR systems. Wikipedia’s inherent structure offers a rich source of background knowledge that can be exploited in several ways. First, Wikipedia’s category system allows for identifying specialized domains within each language. Second, interlingual links between Wikipedia articles provide a natural mechanism for linking related concepts across languages. Constructing large, accurately labeled datasets for gender classification is both time-consuming and, potentially, subject to privacy concerns, while the availability of unlabeled text data is often abundant. This disparity motivates the exploration of semi-supervised learning techniques – paradigms that effectively leverage both labeled and unlabeled data to improve model performance. Existing approaches to gender classification have largely focused on utilizing textual features derived from an author’s writing style, encompassing lexical choices, syntactic patterns, and stylistic characteristics (e.g., Argawal et al., 2009; Schler et al., 2006). While these methods demonstrate promising results, their performance can be limited by the size and quality of the labeled training data. Recent work has begun to explore the integration of social information, particularly leveraging social network connections, to enhance gender prediction accuracy (e.g., Ali et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2017). These approaches typically analyze direct social ties, such as follower/followee relationships, to infer gender similarities among users. However, a crucial observation is that users often connect with each other not necessarily based on shared gender, but rather on shared interests and preferences. This realization motivates a more nuanced approach to incorporating social information, focusing on *indirect* relationships built around common interests. For instance, two users who frequently participate in discussions about a specific hobby or topic are likely to share certain characteristics, potentially including gender-related patterns in their writing. In this paper, we propose a novel semi-supervised approach to gender classification that leverages both textual features and a specific type of indirect social link, termed "same-interest" links. These links are established by identifying users who exhibit overlapping engagement patterns in online communities or shared content consumption. We model the interplay between textual information and these "same-interest" links using a factor graph, termed the Textual and Social Factor Graph (TSFG). This graphical model effectively captures dependencies between user-specific textual features and their connections within the social network, facilitating robust gender prediction even with limited labeled data. Through empirical evaluation on real-world datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, highlighting the benefits of integrating textual and social modeling in a semi-supervised learning framework. We show that the TSFG approach consistently outperforms baseline methods, demonstrating the value of leveraging “same-interest” links for improved gender classification performance. response: Sentiment analysis, the task of computationally determining the opinion or emotion expressed in a piece of text, has become a cornerstone of numerous applications, ranging from brand monitoring and market research to personalized recommendation systems and political analysis. Traditional approaches to sentiment classification often rely on bag-of-words models or term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) representations, neglecting the sequential nature of language and the rich contextual information contained within sentences. More recently, deep learning models, particularly Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have achieved state-of-the-art performance by automatically learning hierarchical representations of text (Socher et al., 2013; Kim, 2014). However, these models typically treat each review in isolation, failing to leverage valuable information about the users who wrote the reviews and the products being reviewed. Incorporating user and product information can significantly enhance sentiment analysis, especially in scenarios where reviews are sparse or ambiguous. For example, knowing that a user consistently provides highly critical reviews may suggest that a seemingly negative sentiment is simply reflective of that user’s overall reviewing style. Similarly, understanding the characteristics of a product – its category, price point, or manufacturer – can provide context for interpreting user opinions. Previous work has attempted to integrate user and product features into sentiment models through various techniques, including feature concatenation (Liu et al., 2012), factorization machines (Rendle & Freudenthaler, 2011), and attention mechanisms (Hong et al., 2018). However, a critical challenge remains largely unaddressed: the *cold-start problem*. In real-world review platforms, a substantial portion of users and products have limited interaction history, resulting in insufficient data to learn reliable representations. For cold-start users or products, simply relying on their own limited data can lead to inaccurate sentiment predictions. Existing models often struggle with this scenario, as they assume the availability of sufficient data for both users and products. To address this limitation, we introduce the Hybrid Contextualized Sentiment Classifier (HCSC). HCSC incorporates a novel Cold-Start Aware Attention (CSAA) mechanism that explicitly considers the cold-start problem when combining word-level representations with user and product embeddings. Our approach utilizes shared vectors constructed from similar users or products, providing a regularizing effect when individual user/product vectors are unreliable due to limited data. A frequency-guided selective gate controls the contribution of these shared vectors, allowing the model to dynamically adapt to the availability of information. We demonstrate through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets that HCSC consistently outperforms existing models, particularly in low-data and cold-start scenarios. Furthermore, our model achieves these performance gains while maintaining competitive computational efficiency, making it suitable for large-scale real-world applications. This work represents a significant step towards building more robust and accurate sentiment analysis systems that can effectively handle the challenges posed by sparse data and cold-start problems.

response: Discriminative training methods have become a cornerstone of modern statistical natural language processing, achieving substantial performance gains over traditional generative approaches (Rosenfeld et al., 1996; Och & Ney, 2002). Among these, Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) (Och, 2003) stands out as a particularly effective technique for optimizing system performance with respect to a task-specific evaluation metric, such as BLEU for machine translation or Word Error Rate (WER) for speech recognition. The core idea behind MERT is to adjust model weights iteratively, favoring hypotheses that yield lower error rates on a development set. However, the optimization landscape presented by typical evaluation metrics is notoriously complex. BLEU and WER, while well-correlated with human judgments, are non-convex, non-differentiable, and often exhibit numerous local optima. The standard MERT algorithm, often employing gradient-based or hill-climbing search strategies, is therefore susceptible to getting trapped in suboptimal solutions. This is particularly concerning as even small improvements in model weights can translate to significant gains in final system performance. In this paper, we address the limitations of conventional MERT algorithms by introducing LP-MERT, an *exact* search algorithm that guarantees finding the globally optimal linear model weights for a given set of N-best lists. Our approach leverages the power of linear programming (LP) to formulate the MERT problem as a set of constraints and an objective function, which can then be solved efficiently and accurately using standard LP solvers. The core innovation lies in a series of reductions – transformations that recast the original, complex problem into a standard linear program. Given N-best lists generated from S input sentences, LP-MERT can determine the linear model parameters that minimize the total error rate across the development set. While theoretically optimal, the computational complexity of LP-MERT presents a considerable challenge. We demonstrate that the algorithm’s runtime is polynomial in N (the size of the N-best lists) and in the model size, but exhibits exponential growth with respect to S (the size of the development set). Recognizing this scalability bottleneck, we explore extensions that enable LP-MERT to handle realistically sized tuning sets. These extensions include strategies for restricting the search space to promising regions of the parameter space and a beam-search approximation that trades off optimality for computational efficiency. Through rigorous experimentation, we demonstrate that LP-MERT consistently outperforms the widely used Och algorithm (Och, 2003) in terms of both optimization accuracy and downstream system performance. This work represents a significant step towards unlocking the full potential of discriminative training in NLP by providing a provably optimal method for model parameter estimation. response: The rapid growth of microblogging platforms like Twitter has created a wealth of user-generated content, offering a unique window into public opinion, emerging trends, and real-time events. However, the sheer volume and velocity of tweets pose significant challenges for effective information summarization and analysis. Unlike traditional document-centric text, Twitter data is characterized by its brevity, noisy nature, and dynamic topicality. Consequently, methods developed for summarizing longer, more formal texts often struggle to effectively capture the essence of Twitter conversations. response: Coreference resolution, the task of identifying mentions in text that refer to the same entity, is a fundamental problem in natural language processing with broad applications in information extraction, machine translation, and question answering. Despite decades of research, achieving high accuracy on this task remains a significant challenge, particularly in complex and diverse text genres. The prevailing paradigm in contemporary coreference resolution systems is to frame the problem as a series of binary classification tasks (Soon et al., 2001; Aone & Neeleman, 2003; Bengtson & Kübler, 2004). Specifically, each pair of mentions within a document is assessed for whether they are coreferent or not. This effectively transforms the complex, multi-way coreference problem into a manageable set of simpler pairwise decisions. These classification approaches typically leverage supervised machine learning algorithms, trained on annotated corpora, to predict the coreference link between mention pairs. Common algorithms employed include support vector machines (SVMs), logistic regression, and more recently, neural network-based models (Clark & Manning, 2015; Lee et al., 2017). These algorithms are optimized to minimize classification errors – i.e., to correctly classify as many mention pairs as coreferent or non-coreferent as possible on the training data. However, a crucial disconnect exists between the training objective – minimizing classification error – and the evaluation metric used to assess coreference resolution performance. Standard metrics like the MUC score (Vilain & Burger, 1997) and B-CUBED (Bagga & Baliukas, 1998) are based on evaluating the overall quality of the identified coreference chains, rather than simply counting correct pairwise decisions. A system that optimizes for classification accuracy may not necessarily optimize for performance on these holistic evaluation metrics. This is because misclassifying certain high-confidence errors can have a disproportionately negative impact on the evaluation metric score, while correctly classifying numerous low-confidence pairs may yield minimal improvement. This discrepancy motivates the need for training approaches that directly optimize the evaluation metric of interest. Previous work has explored techniques for metric learning (Chang et al., 2008; Ratinov & Roth, 2009), but these often require modifications to the learning algorithm or introduce computational complexity. The vast majority of research and evaluation, however, has concentrated on formal, well-structured text, such as news articles (Papineni et al., 2002), parliamentary proceedings (Tiedemann, 2009), and technical manuals. Translating informal text, particularly conversational dialogues, presents a distinct set of challenges that have historically received considerably less attention. This disparity is particularly notable given the increasing prominence of dialogue in everyday communication, from social media interactions to customer service chatbots, and the growing demand for MT systems capable of handling these more nuanced and context-dependent language styles. Conversational text differs fundamentally from formal text in several key aspects. It relies heavily on context, incorporates pragmatic cues, and often features incomplete sentences, colloquialisms, and a wide range of stylistic variations. Furthermore, dialogues are characterized by features intrinsic to the conversational setting itself - specifically, the identity of the speakers, their respective dialogue acts (e.g., questions, statements, commands), and the overall register (e.g., formal, informal, vulgar). Ignoring these conversational aspects can lead to translations that are grammatically correct but pragmatically inappropriate, lacking the subtle nuances and stylistic features that characterize natural dialogue. Previous work has explored the adaptation of MT systems to specific domains (Kuhn and Knight, 2002) and styles (Michel et al., 2008). However, a systematic investigation of the influence of *conversational* aspects on MT quality is still largely lacking. Existing resources for MT often lack the fine-grained annotations necessary to analyze these nuances, hindering research in this area. response: Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has seen remarkable progress in recent years, largely driven by advances in phrase-based models (Koehn et al., 2003). However, a key bottleneck remains the computational cost of decoding, particularly for long and complex sentences. While significant effort has been devoted to optimizing phrase table construction and search algorithms, relatively little attention has been given to improving the efficiency of syntactic computations within the decoder. This is somewhat surprising, given the demonstrated benefits of incorporating syntactic information into SMT systems (Yamada & Knight, 2001; Chiang, 2005; Nivre & McDonald, 2008). Traditionally, syntactic analyses, specifically dependency parses, have been computationally expensive operations, typically requiring cubic time complexity with respect to sentence length. This cost has limited their practical application in real-time MT decoding scenarios. Recent work by McDonald et al. (2005b) presented a crucial shift in this landscape. They recast dependency parsing as a maximum spanning tree (MST) problem, a graph-theoretic formulation that allows for efficient quadratic-time solutions. Importantly, their experiments demonstrated that MST parsing achieves accuracy levels comparable to traditional, cubic-time parsing methods, particularly for English. Furthermore, they observed improved accuracy with languages exhibiting freer word order, where dependency structures are less constrained. This finding is particularly relevant to machine translation, where source language syntax can significantly differ from target language syntax. This paper explores the integration of quadratic-time MST parsing into a phrase-based SMT decoder. We hypothesize that augmenting a phrase-based system with a dependency language model (DLM) computed via MST parsing will yield improved translation quality without incurring a prohibitive computational cost. Our approach involves leveraging the dependency structure to score translation hypotheses, favoring those that conform to grammatically plausible dependencies in the target language. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through experiments on five NIST Chinese-English evaluation test sets. The results showcase significant improvements in both Translation Error Rate (TER) and BLEU scores, demonstrating the potential of efficient syntactic parsing for enhancing SMT performance. Specifically, we achieve a 0.92% reduction in TER and a 0.45% increase in BLEU, highlighting the benefits of incorporating readily available, accurate, and efficient dependency information into the translation process. This work therefore bridges a gap between advancements in parsing efficiency and their practical application within the challenging context of machine translation decoding. It is important to note that while previous work (Nivre & McDonald, 2008) has investigated dependency parsing in SMT, those approaches typically relied on computationally expensive cubic-time parsers, limiting their scalability. response: Transliteration, the task of converting a word from one script to another while preserving its pronunciation, is a crucial component in many multilingual natural language processing systems. It serves as a bridge between languages with different writing systems, enabling applications such as cross-lingual information retrieval, speech recognition, and, crucially, machine translation (MT). Traditional approaches to transliteration largely relied on rule-based systems or statistical models based on character-level mappings (Koehn & Knight, 2002; Li et al., 2002). However, these systems often struggle with out-of-vocabulary words and the complexities of pronunciation variations. More recently, the application of discriminative methods, pioneered by Sherif and Kondrak (2007a, 2007b), has demonstrated significant improvements in transliteration accuracy. These discriminative approaches typically frame transliteration as a character transduction problem, learning to map source-language character sequences to target-language character sequences. While promising, existing discriminative methods often lack mechanisms to leverage readily available knowledge about potential target-language words. In real-world transliteration scenarios, one frequently has access to a list of valid words in the target language – a lexicon – which can dramatically constrain the search space and improve accuracy. In this paper, we present a novel discriminative substring decoder for transliteration that explicitly incorporates this lexicon information. Our decoder builds upon the foundation laid by Sherif and Kondrak (2007b), but extends it to allow for a list of known target-language words during the decoding process. By incorporating this constraint, the decoder can effectively prioritize candidate transliterations that correspond to valid words, leading to substantial gains in accuracy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a challenging Japanese katakana-to-English transliteration task, achieving a 28.5% relative improvement over the state-of-the-art. Furthermore, we investigate the relative merits of two dominant feature paradigms for discriminative training: indicator features and hybrid generative features (Taskar et al., 2005). Indicator features provide a purely discriminative approach, directly representing the presence or absence of linguistic properties. Hybrid generative features, on the other hand, combine discriminative modeling with insights derived from generative models. Surprisingly, we find that the hybrid generative features consistently outperform their purely discriminative counterparts, despite sacrificing access to rich source-context features traditionally used in discriminative models. This suggests that the generative component provides valuable inductive bias in the transliteration task. Finally, we explore the downstream impact of improved transliteration on a larger task: machine translation. The core strength of HPB lies in its ability to represent long-distance reorderings through tree-like structures, offering a more flexible and expressive modeling capability than simple phrase reordering tables. However, a significant limitation of conventional HPB systems is their reliance on largely context-independent reordering decisions. response: Automatic keyphrase extraction (AKE) aims to identify the most important phrases within a document that capture its salient content. This task has numerous applications, including document summarization, information retrieval, and search engine optimization. Evaluating the performance of AKE systems is a crucial step in their development, enabling researchers to compare different approaches and track progress. Traditionally, AKE systems are evaluated using metrics that rely on exact matches between extracted keyphrases and a set of reference keyphrases provided by human annotators. Common metrics include precision, recall, and F1-score. However, these standard metrics are known to be strict and often fail to capture partial overlaps or near-misses – instances where the extracted keyphrase is semantically similar to a reference keyphrase but does not match exactly. For example, an extracted keyphrase of “machine learning algorithms” might be considered incorrect by a metric requiring exact matching, even if a reference keyphrase is “machine learning techniques.” This limitation motivates the exploration of more flexible evaluation metrics that can account for semantic similarity and partial matches. Inspired by the fields of machine translation and text summarization, where dealing with variations in wording is commonplace, we investigate the feasibility of adapting n-gram-based evaluation metrics for AKE. These metrics, such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and ROUGE (Lin, 2004), consider overlapping n-grams between the generated text and the reference text, providing a more nuanced assessment of quality. We hypothesize that incorporating such metrics into the evaluation of AKE systems will provide a more accurate and informative picture of their performance. In this paper, we conduct a feasibility study that explores a range of n-gram-based evaluation metrics for AKE, including adaptations of BLEU, ROUGE, and R-precision (Allan, 1996) – a metric originally designed for keyphrase evaluation. Through empirical evaluation on a benchmark dataset, we compare the correlation of these metrics with human annotations to determine which provides the most reliable assessment of AKE system performance. Our findings demonstrate that R-precision, when appropriately adjusted for keyphrase evaluation, consistently achieves the highest correlation with human judgments. Furthermore, we present evidence suggesting that the degree of semantic similarity captured by these metrics is influenced by the position of the partially-matching component words within the keyphrases. This insight has implications for the design of more sophisticated n-gram-based metrics that can better capture the semantic relationships between extracted and reference keyphrases. The goal of this work is not to replace existing evaluation methods, but to augment them with approaches that are less sensitive to surface form variation and provide a more comprehensive assessment of AKE system capabilities. While sentence-level sentiment analysis has seen substantial progress, scaling this understanding to the document level requires reasoning about relationships between multiple entities and navigating complex interactions. Existing methods frequently focus on sentiment expressed within individual sentences (Socher et al., 2013;Kim, 2014), often overlooking crucial contextual information that spans the entire document. This limitation becomes particularly acute when dealing with nuanced opinions and implicit sentiments, where understanding the broader context is essential for accurate inference. A key aspect often missing in document-level sentiment analysis is the recognition that opinions are rarely formed in a vacuum. Social dynamics, affiliations, and inherent biases significantly influence attitudes and expressions. For example, a news article discussing a merger between two companies might not explicitly state the sentiment of the CEOs involved, but the reader intuitively understands that their opinions are likely aligned with the strategic goals of their respective organizations. Capturing such implicit relationships necessitates incorporating knowledge about entity factions, social networks, and established principles of social behavior. Previous work in document-level sentiment often relies on limited supervision, typically focusing on entity pairs explicitly mentioned within the same sentence (Abadie et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2013). For instance, an ontology designed for general language understanding might lack the nuanced distinctions required for specialized tasks like biomedical information extraction or clinical decision support. This disconnect between design and application is a common challenge. Traditionally, a dominant approach has focused on the ‘linguistic turn,’ positing that meaning emerges primarily from relationships *within* language itself. This view, championed by distributional semantic models (Lund & Feifer, 1991; Mikolov et al., 2013), suggests that the meaning of a word can be inferred from the company it keeps – the surrounding words (its ‘distribution’) within vast textual corpora. These models have undeniably proven powerful in capturing semantic similarities and relationships, achieving remarkable success in tasks like word analogy and semantic relatedness judgments. However, a growing body of evidence challenges the assumption that meaning is solely derived from linguistic context. The embodied cognition perspective (Barsalou, 2008; Glenberg & Gallese, 2005) argues that conceptual knowledge is fundamentally grounded in perceptual and motor experience. This means our understanding of a word like “kick” isn’t simply a matter of its co-occurrence with words like “ball” and “foot,” but also incorporates the sensorimotor simulation of *performing* the act of kicking—the feeling of leg muscles contracting, the visual image of a foot striking an object, and so on. This perspective suggests that language is not a self-contained system, but rather interfaces with, and is shaped by, our interactions with the physical world. Despite the theoretical appeal of grounded cognition, integrating perceptual information into computational models of semantics has proven challenging. Simply adding perceptual features to existing linguistic models often yields limited improvements, or even degrades performance (Binder & Westphal, 2005). These parameters, typically feature weights controlling various aspects of the translation process – from phrase translation probabilities to distortion penalties – significantly impact translation quality. It struggles with systems incorporating a large number of features – a common scenario in modern SMT – due to the computationally intensive nature of its optimization process. Furthermore, MERT’s optimization landscape can be complex, leading to local optima and inconsistent results. More recent work has explored online learning approaches, leveraging algorithms like MIRA (Margin-Infused Relaxed Algorithm) developed by Crammer and Singer (2003). Approaches building on MIRA, such as those proposed by Watanabe et al. (2007) and Chiang et al. (2008b), demonstrate improved performance and scalability compared to MERT. However, despite their impressive performance, NMT models often face challenges related to training instability and a discrepancy between training and inference procedures. A key issue stems from the typical training objective used in NMT – the cross-entropy loss calculated at the word level. This loss function operates under the assumption that the model can accurately predict each word given the preceding ground-truth words (teacher forcing). While computationally efficient, this approach has several drawbacks. First, it evaluates the translation quality solely based on individual word predictions, neglecting the overall fluency and adequacy of the generated sequence. More critically, teacher forcing creates a significant mismatch between the training and inference phases. During training, the model is always provided with correct preceding words, while at inference, it must rely on its own previously generated words as context – a phenomenon known as “exposure bias” (Bengio et al., 2015). This bias can lead to compounding errors during decoding, where initial mistakes propagate and degrade the quality of the entire translation. Several approaches have been proposed to address these limitations. One promising direction is sequence-level training, where the model is directly optimized for metrics that correlate better with translation quality, such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). However, directly optimizing non-differentiable metrics like BLEU is challenging. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a framework to overcome this obstacle by treating the translation process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and training the model to maximize expected reward (Ranzato et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016). response: Machine translation (MT) systems typically rely on a pipeline architecture comprising several stages: tokenization, word alignment, phrase extraction, and decoding. While significant progress has been made in each of these components, the initial tokenization step often receives comparatively less attention, particularly for languages where the segmentation of text into meaningful units is ambiguous. This is especially true for languages like Chinese, Korean, and Thai, where words are not explicitly delimited by spaces. The ambiguity inherent in tokenization—the same character sequence can often be split into different word segments—presents a significant challenge for MT systems that rely on 1-best tokenizations. A poorly chosen tokenization can fundamentally alter the meaning of a sentence and subsequently lead to translation errors. Traditional approaches to handling tokenization ambiguity in MT often involve generating a lattice of possible tokenizations. A lattice, in this context, represents all plausible segmentations of the source sentence, each with an associated probability. The MT decoder then operates on this lattice, exploring multiple tokenization options during the search for the best translation. While the lattice approach effectively mitigates the problem of 1-best tokenization errors, it introduces increased computational complexity, as the decoder now needs to navigate a significantly larger search space. Furthermore, the creation of the lattice itself often relies on a separate monolingual tokenizer, whose errors can propagate into the MT system. response: Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) aims to identify the predicate-argument structure of a sentence, effectively answering "who did what to whom, when, where, and how” (Gildea and Jurafsky, 2002). It’s a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing, crucial for applications like information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. Traditionally, SRL research has largely focused on two prominent datasets: PropBank (Palmer et al., 2005) and NomBank (Meyers et al., 2004). PropBank annotates verb-centric predicate-argument structures, focusing on actions and events described by verbal predicates. NomBank, conversely, annotates noun-centric structures, addressing arguments related to nominal predicates – events or states realized by nouns. Despite the distinct nature of these datasets, a unified approach to SRL offers significant advantages. A single, integrated system avoids the need for separate pipelines for verbal and nominal predicates, potentially leveraging shared knowledge and reducing error propagation. Moreover, a holistic view of predicate-argument structures improves semantic understanding of the sentence. However, building such an integrated system presents substantial challenges. The differing annotation schemes, predicate types, and argument sets necessitate careful consideration during system design and feature engineering. Existing approaches to SRL have often adopted a pipeline architecture, independently processing PropBank and NomBank and then combining the results. While these pipeline systems have achieved reasonable performance (Surdeanu et al., 2008; Johnson and Klein, 2009), they suffer from inherent limitations. Errors in the initial stages can cascade through the pipeline, negatively impacting overall accuracy. Furthermore, pipeline systems struggle to capture complex interactions between verbal and nominal predications within a single sentence. Recent work has explored dependency-based SRL, framing the task as identifying semantic relationships within a dependency parse tree (Marneffe et al., 2006). This approach offers several benefits, including a more natural representation of semantic roles and the ability to leverage syntactic information effectively. However, the success of dependency-based SRL heavily relies on the careful selection of informative features. In this paper, we present a novel dependency-based SRL system that integrates PropBank and NomBank annotations. Our approach distinguishes itself through a rigorous feature selection process, utilizing a large-scale feature template set and employing a technique to identify the most discriminative features for accurate semantic role labeling. By introducing “assistant argument labels” – features designed to better capture contextual information – and strategically discerning optimal feature subsets, we construct a high-performance single SRL system that achieves competitive results on the CoNLL-2008 shared task dataset. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first integrated SRL system capable of achieving performance comparable to previously established pipeline systems, demonstrating the effectiveness of our integrated approach and efficient feature selection methodology. We demonstrate not merely an integration of two datasets, but a synergistic improvement born from their combined analysis.

Early ATS systems relied heavily on surface-level features such as essay length, word count, and grammatical error detection (Landauer et al., 1998; Foltz et al., 1999). Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), have opened new avenues for ATS. Neural network models, capable of learning complex patterns directly from data, offer the potential to overcome the limitations of traditional feature engineering approaches (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; Cho et al., 2014). This demand drives a need for automated terminology acquisition (TA) systems capable of identifying and extracting these terms from large volumes of text. While parallel corpora (texts and their direct translations) provide a goldmine for terminology translation, they are often expensive and time-consuming to create, particularly for highly specialized domains. response: Textual Entailment (TE) is a fundamental problem in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that assesses whether the meaning of one text fragment (the text, T) can be inferred from another (the hypothesis, H). Formally, T entails H if a human reading T would reasonably conclude that H is true. This task has gained significant attention due to its broad applicability to various NLP applications, including question answering, information retrieval, and machine translation evaluation (Manning, 2008; MacDorman, 2009). The core challenge of TE lies in determining semantic relationships between textual units, requiring a deep understanding of lexical semantics, compositional semantics, and world knowledge. While much of the initial research focused on monolingual TE, the increasing demand for cross-lingual information access has motivated substantial effort in the area of Cross-Lingual Textual Entailment (CLTE). CLTE extends the traditional TE task to scenarios where the text and hypothesis are written in different languages. This introduces the additional complexity of bridging the lexical and semantic gaps between languages, making CLTE a particularly challenging problem. Existing approaches to CLTE broadly fall into two categories: machine translation-based methods and direct comparison methods (Schulte im Hof, 2010). Machine translation-based methods translate either the text or the hypothesis into the language of the other, and then perform monolingual TE. Direct comparison methods, on the other hand, attempt to establish entailment relationships directly, without relying on full translation. This paper investigates the potential of leveraging bilingual parallel corpora – collections of sentences and their translations – as a valuable resource for CLTE. We hypothesize that phrase tables, automatically extracted from these corpora, can provide essential lexical knowledge for cross-lingual inference. These phrase tables go beyond simple word-to-word translations, capturing multi-word expressions and contextual information that can significantly enhance the accuracy of entailment judgments. The advantages of using parallel corpora are threefold: First, they offer a readily available, often large-scale, source of lexical knowledge for various language pairs. Second, the parallel nature of the data inherently captures translational equivalences, providing a robust basis for cross-lingual comparison. Third, phrase tables explicitly model relationships between phrases, effectively capturing contextual information absent in simple dictionary-based lookup approaches. By focusing solely on phrasal matching, we aim to minimize interference from other inference mechanisms and gain a clearer understanding of the impact of lexical information on CLTE performance. We conduct experiments on an English-Spanish corpus derived from the Recognizing Textual Entailment (RTE3) shared task, and demonstrate that our method achieves accuracy levels comparable to, and even exceeding, many systems reported in the RTE3 competition on monolingual data. Furthermore, we show that utilizing parallel corpora for extracting paraphrase tables can improve performance even in the monolingual setting, suggesting the broader utility of this resource for semantic relatedness tasks.

CN-decoding operates by constructing a directed acyclic graph, the confusion network, representing the possible translation options proposed by multiple MT systems. Nodes in the graph represent word segments, and edges denote alignment links between corresponding segments across different hypotheses. The network is then searched to identify the most probable translation path, effectively integrating the diverse outputs of the contributing systems. However, the success of CN-decoding hinges critically on the accuracy of *hypothesis alignment*. This process identifies corresponding segments across the different MT system outputs, creating the necessary edges within the confusion network. A fundamental challenge in hypothesis alignment lies in the frequent discrepancies in word order exhibited by different MT systems. These variations can arise from differences in model architectures, training data, or decoding strategies, and can significantly hinder the identification of accurate alignment links. Numerous approaches to hypothesis alignment have been proposed, relying on various techniques such as word alignment (GIZA++ (Och & Ney, 2003), TER (Snover et al., 2006)), string alignment (CLA (Yang et al., 2011)), and Hidden Markov Models (IHMM (Yamamoto & Neubig, 2012)). Our experimental results demonstrate that intersection word alignment consistently yields performance improvements across all four base word alignment methods. This suggests that integrating both direct and inverse alignment information is a valuable strategy for addressing the challenges of hypothesis alignment in MT system combination.

Consequently, the need for robust and reliable evaluation methodologies has become increasingly crucial. Traditionally, the quality of generated text has been assessed through correlation with human judgments – relying on metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), ROUGE (Lin, 2004), and more recently, learned metrics based on neural networks (Shang et al., 2015; Gehring et al., 2017). A well-documented observation (Papineni et al., 2002;Koehn, 2004;Callison-Burch et al., 2006) is that human assessments of text quality exhibit considerable variability and a lack of inter-annotator agreement. This inconsistency casts doubt on the validity of relying solely on correlation with human judgment as the gold standard for metric evaluation. response: Information Retrieval (IR) systems have long relied on statistical models to assess the relevance of documents to a given query. Traditional approaches, such as the Boolean model and Vector Space Model (VSM), often focus on exact term matching or weighted term frequencies. However, these methods frequently struggle with issues of synonymy and polysemy – the presence of multiple words with similar meanings, and the existence of words with multiple meanings, respectively. A user’s intent when posing a query rarely aligns perfectly with the exact terms used in relevant documents. Consequently, effective IR requires a mechanism to overcome lexical mismatch and capture the underlying semantic relationships between terms. Existing techniques to address this challenge often involve query expansion, where related terms are added to the original query to broaden the search scope. These approaches, while helpful, typically rely on manually constructed thesauri (e.g., WordNet) or statistical co-occurrence measures, which can be limited in coverage and prone to noise. Furthermore, such methods often lack a probabilistic foundation, making it difficult to effectively integrate them into a principled IR framework. In this paper, we present a novel probabilistic model, the Hierarchical Dirichlet Tree (HDT), designed to capture similarities amongst terms directly within the generative process of document and query representation. The HDT leverages a tree structure over the vocabulary, where nodes represent clusters of semantically related terms. By modeling the distribution of terms within this hierarchy, the HDT implicitly performs a form of query expansion, retrieving documents based on not only the query terms themselves, but also terms deemed similar based on their position within the tree. Importantly, our framework is grounded in a principled generative probabilistic model. This allows us to not only capture term similarities, but also to naturally exhibit an effect analogous to Inverse Document Frequency (IDF), a crucial component of many successful IR systems. Documents containing rare and informative terms are given higher relevance scores. We demonstrate, through experimental evaluation on standard IR benchmarks, that the HDT consistently outperforms traditional IR baselines. These results suggest that our hierarchical model provides a compelling alternative to existing methods, offering a robust and flexible means of capturing semantic relationships and improving retrieval performance. response: Machine translation (MT) systems typically rely on word-level alignment between source and target languages. However, for many languages, particularly those without explicit word delimiters like Chinese and Arabic, the notion of a "word" is ambiguous, and the performance of MT systems can be significantly hindered by incorrect or suboptimal word segmentation. Traditional approaches to this problem often involve manually defined rules or statistically trained segmenters based on monolingual corpora, sometimes followed by iterative refinement using bilingual data. While these methods can be effective, they frequently require substantial linguistic expertise and can be brittle when applied to new domains or language pairs. Recent advancements in statistical machine translation have shown the potential of jointly learning segmentation and alignment. However, many existing joint models make strong parametric assumptions about the underlying distributions. For example, hierarchical phrase-based translation models implicitly impose a segmentation structure based on the learned phrase table. This can limit the flexibility of the model and may not be optimal for all languages. Furthermore, such models can be computationally expensive to train, particularly for large-scale datasets. In this paper, we propose a novel nonparametric approach to word segmentation for machine translation. Our model leverages the strengths of existing monolingual segmentation techniques, such as those based on character-level language models or minimum description length principles, while simultaneously incorporating information from the target sentence through a bilingual word alignment model. Critically, we avoid making strong parametric assumptions about the segmentation distribution, allowing the model to adapt more readily to the specific characteristics of the language pair and domain. Our approach frames word segmentation as an inference problem where the segmentation of the source sentence is guided by the alignments to the target sentence. Specifically, we couple the monolingual segmentation model and the bilingual word alignment model during inference. The alignment model provides feedback to the segmentation model, favoring segmentations that yield higher-quality alignments to the target sentence. This iterative process allows the model to refine both the segmentation and alignment simultaneously, leading to improved translation performance. We evaluate our approach on Arabic-English and Chinese-English translation tasks. The experimental results demonstrate that our nonparametric word segmentation model consistently outperforms baseline systems that rely on fixed, independently trained segmenters. This suggests that jointly learning segmentation and alignment, even with a relatively simple coupling mechanism, can significantly benefit machine translation quality for languages with ambiguous word boundaries. Our findings contribute to the growing body of work on unsupervised methods for handling morphological complexity in machine translation and offer a promising direction for future research in this area. These reviews are critical for both consumers – aiding purchasing decisions – and businesses – offering valuable feedback and influencing reputation. However, the sheer scale of this data presents significant challenges. A fundamental task in harnessing this data is identifying *review pages* – those containing actual product or service evaluations – versus other types of web pages (e.g., product description pages, help forums, or even unrelated content). Manually labeling these pages is a time-consuming and expensive undertaking, especially when dealing with websites containing millions of pages. This bottleneck severely limits the scalability of many downstream natural language processing (NLP) applications that rely on clean, labeled review datasets, such as sentiment analysis, aspect-based summarization, and fake review detection. Existing approaches to identifying review pages largely fall into the realm of supervised learning. These methods typically train classifiers using features extracted from web page content and structure. However, the performance of these classifiers is fundamentally limited by the availability of labeled training data. Obtaining such data often requires costly human annotation, negating the benefits of processing large volumes of web-scraped content. Semi-supervised methods offer some relief, leveraging a small amount of labeled data alongside a larger pool of unlabeled data, but still ultimately rely on an initial human labeling effort. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to identifying review pages that entirely eliminates the need for human labels. Our method centers around two core principles. First, we exploit the abundance of *noisy* labels available through web scraping. By applying simple heuristics – such as keyword searches for “review,” “rating,” or “customer feedback” – we can automatically label a large number of pages. While these heuristics are imperfect and generate significant noise, the sheer volume of data allows us to build a reasonably effective initial classifier. Second, we leverage the inherent *structure* of websites. Review pages often exhibit characteristic HTML patterns, contain specific review-related elements (e.g., star ratings, review submission forms), and are linked to product pages in a consistent manner. We integrate these structural features into our classifier to improve its accuracy and robustness. Our experiments, conducted on a large-scale dataset of web pages, demonstrate that our label-free method achieves competitive performance compared to supervised learning approaches that require extensive human annotation. response: The ability to automatically transfer linguistic knowledge across languages is a central goal in natural language processing. Such transfer learning is especially valuable for languages with limited annotated resources, where training high-performance models directly is often infeasible. A common paradigm for cross-lingual transfer is *direct transfer*, where a model trained on a resource-rich language (typically English) is directly applied to a resource-poor language. However, the performance of direct transfer systems is often hampered by differences in linguistic structure and vocabulary between the source and target languages. Recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of incorporating word cluster features, learned from large unlabeled corpora, to improve the prediction of linguistic structure in monolingual settings (Pereira et al., 2003; Miller et al., 2004). These word clusters capture semantic and syntactic regularities, providing valuable contextual information for downstream tasks. While these approaches have shown promising results for English, their applicability to other languages and, more crucially, their potential for improving cross-lingual transfer have remained largely unexplored. In this paper, we address these gaps by investigating the benefits of word clusters for cross-lingual structure prediction. We first demonstrate that the advantages of word cluster features extend beyond English, holding true for a diverse set of languages across different families. More importantly, we introduce a novel algorithm for *inducing cross-lingual word clusters* – that is, clusters which are aligned across languages in a manner that reflects shared linguistic properties. This approach enables us to directly transfer information learned from unlabeled data in one language to improve structure prediction in another. We evaluate our cross-lingual clustering algorithm by augmenting direct transfer systems for two core NLP tasks: delexicalized dependency parsing and named entity recognition (NER). Our results demonstrate significant performance gains. Specifically, by incorporating cross-lingual cluster features, we reduce the relative error of delexicalized dependency parsers trained on English treebanks and transferred to foreign languages by up to 13%. Furthermore, we observe relative improvements of up to 26% when applying the same method to direct transfer of named-entity recognizers. These improvements highlight the powerful potential of leveraging unlabeled data for cross-lingual transfer, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for aligning linguistic knowledge across languages. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work on cross-lingual transfer and word cluster models. Section 3 details our algorithm for inducing cross-lingual word clusters. Section 4 presents our experimental setup and results. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and discusses future work.
