response: Understanding the temporal ordering of events is fundamental to comprehending narrative and discourse. Humans effortlessly interpret when events occur in relation to one another – whether one precedes, follows, overlaps, or is simultaneous with another. Automatically identifying these temporal relations, however, remains a significant challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP). This task is critical for a broad range of applications, including information extraction, question answering, machine translation, and summarization, all of which require a nuanced understanding of event sequencing. Early approaches to temporal relation classification predominantly focused on identifying six core relations: BEFORE, AFTER, OVERLAP, BEGINS, ENDS, and DURING (Allen, 1983). These relations, while capturing essential temporal information, often lack the granularity needed for detailed discourse analysis. The TimeBank corpus (Pustejovsky et al., 2003), a widely-used resource for temporal reasoning, defines a more comprehensive set of 14 temporal relations, including instances of equality, relative time, and more precise overlaps. Despite the availability of this richer annotation scheme, many existing systems continue to collapse these relations into the six broader categories, sacrificing valuable information. Furthermore, a common thread in much of the prior work is a reliance on shallow, morpho-syntactic features. Systems frequently leverage cues such as tense, aspect, and temporal adverbs to infer temporal orderings. While undeniably useful, these superficial features often prove insufficient to accurately classify nuanced temporal relations, particularly in cases where explicit temporal markers are absent or ambiguous. A deeper understanding of semantic and discourse context is often required. In this paper, we present a novel approach to temporal relation classification that addresses these limitations. We depart from the six-relation paradigm and tackle the task of classifying event-event or event-time pairs into all 14 temporal relations as defined by TimeBank. Crucially, we incorporate rich linguistic knowledge derived from a diverse range of semantic and discourse relations, moving beyond a reliance on purely morpho-syntactic cues. This knowledge encompasses information about event types, causal relationships, and coreference, enabling a more informed assessment of temporal order. Finally, we introduce a hybrid system that synergistically combines the strengths of rule-based and learning-based approaches. Rule-based systems excel at capturing precise linguistic patterns, while learning-based systems demonstrate robustness and adaptability. By integrating these two paradigms, we aim to mitigate the weaknesses of each and create a more powerful and accurate temporal relation classifier. Our experiments on the TimeBank corpus demonstrate that this knowledge-rich, hybrid approach yields a substantial 15-16% relative reduction in error compared to a state-of-the-art learning-based baseline system, highlighting the benefits of our integrated methodology. We believe this work represents a significant step towards more reliable and nuanced temporal reasoning in NLP. Allen, J. F. (1983). response: Neural machine translation (NMT) has rapidly emerged as the dominant paradigm for machine translation, offering a compelling end-to-end learning framework that bypasses many of the complexities inherent in traditional statistical machine translation (SMT) systems (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014). However, a notable drawback of NMT is its insatiable appetite for model capacity. Achieving state-of-the-art translation quality typically necessitates exceedingly large models with millions, or even billions, of parameters. Such models present significant challenges in terms of computational cost, memory requirements, and deployment feasibility, particularly in resource-constrained environments. Recent advancements in machine learning have explored techniques for model compression, aiming to reduce the size and complexity of large neural networks without substantial performance degradation. Among the most promising approaches is knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015; Bucila et al., 2006), wherein a smaller “student” model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained “teacher” model. This allows the student to benefit from the knowledge embedded within the teacher, enabling it to achieve comparable performance with fewer parameters. Knowledge distillation has found success in various domains, including image classification and speech recognition, but its application to NMT has received comparatively less attention. In this paper, we investigate the effectiveness of knowledge distillation for compressing NMT models. We begin by demonstrating that applying standard knowledge distillation techniques, focused on mimicking the teacher’s word-level prediction probabilities, can indeed lead to substantial reductions in model size with minimal impact on translation quality. However, we observe that the full potential of knowledge distillation lies in going beyond simple output matching. Therefore, we introduce two novel sequence-level knowledge distillation methods that operate directly on the entire translated sequence, rather than individual words. These methods encourage the student model to not only predict the correct words, but also to generate sequences that are structurally and semantically similar to those produced by the teacher. Our experiments confirm that entity-balanced clusters are strongly preferred by users. These findings highlight the potential of sequence-level knowledge distillation as a powerful tool for building efficient and high-performing NMT systems.

A poorly classified question can lead to irrelevant information retrieval, incorrect answer extraction, or even system failure. Early approaches to question classification heavily relied on feature engineering and machine learning algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) (Joachims, 1998) and Naive Bayes (Sebastiani, 2002). These methods typically employed features derived from lexical characteristics, syntactic patterns, and semantic information extracted from the question text. More recently, deep learning models like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (Kim, 2014) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) have gained prominence in question classification. These models are capable of automatically learning relevant features from raw text data, reducing the reliance on manual feature engineering. response: Maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) has long served as the cornerstone of training structured prediction models across a wide spectrum of natural language processing (NLP) tasks involving text generation, including machine translation, text summarization, and dialogue systems (Bengio et al., 2003; Sutskever et al., 2014). While conceptually straightforward and computationally efficient, MLE training is increasingly recognized to suffer from inherent limitations, particularly when evaluated against sequence-level metrics. A primary concern is *exposure bias*: during training, the model only sees ground-truth prefixes, but during inference, it generates its own, potentially error-prone prefixes. This discrepancy can lead to accumulated errors and degraded performance. Another, often overlooked, issue is the *objective mismatch* – MLE optimizes for word-level correctness (predicting the next token), while evaluation fundamentally occurs at the sequence level, using discrete metrics like ROUGE (Lin, 2004) and BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). Recent research has explored alternatives to MLE, predominantly within the realm of reinforcement learning (RL) and policy gradient methods, aiming to directly optimize for these evaluation metrics (Ranzato et al., 2016; Bahdanau et al., 2017). These approaches treat the sequence generation process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), and learn a policy to maximize expected reward, where the reward is typically a sequence-level metric. While promising, policy gradient methods are notoriously challenging to train. The high variance inherent in estimating rewards, especially for long sequences, leads to unstable training dynamics and often necessitates complex variance reduction techniques (Williams, 1992). Furthermore, the non-differentiable nature of discrete evaluation metrics requires approximating the gradient, introducing additional noise and instability. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to sequence-level optimization that bypasses the challenges of policy gradient methods while still addressing the limitations of MLE. We introduce CALCS (Continuously Approximating Longest Common Subsequence), a new training objective based on a differentiable surrogate of the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) measure. LCS, unlike ROUGE or BLEU, provides a continuous measure of similarity between generated and reference sequences, allowing for direct gradient-based optimization. CALCS continuously approximates the LCS between the generated sequence and the reference sequence, employing a soft alignment mechanism that enables efficient backpropagation. By maximizing CALCS, the model learns to generate sequences that are structurally similar to the references, capturing the crucial sequence-level relationships that are often missed by MLE. Our experiments on both abstractive summarization and machine translation demonstrate the effectiveness of CALCS. We show that models trained with CALCS consistently outperform those trained with MLE, and achieve competitive results compared to existing policy gradient approaches, but with significantly more stable and efficient training. We believe that CALCS offers a compelling alternative for sequence-level optimization, bridging the gap between the simplicity of MLE and the accuracy of reinforcement learning.

Given two sentences – a premise and a hypothesis – the goal of NLI is to determine the relationship between them: whether the hypothesis is entailed by the premise, contradicted by the premise, or neutral relative to the premise. This task requires a deep understanding of semantics, reasoning, and world knowledge, making it a significant benchmark for evaluating the capabilities of NLP models. Recent advances in NLI have been largely driven by neural network architectures, particularly those leveraging the attention mechanism. Models like the Attentive Reader (Rocktäschel et al., 2016) and the Enhanced Sequential Inference Model (ESIM) (Chen et al., 2016) employ attention to selectively focus on relevant parts of the premises when processing the hypothesis, effectively capturing interactions between the two sentences. These attention-based models have achieved state-of-the-art results on several NLI datasets. However, the success of attention mechanisms is not without limitations. While effective at highlighting important relationships, attention often focuses on lexical overlap and may struggle with more complex, nuanced interactions that are not immediately apparent through surface-level matching. Moreover, attention mechanisms typically operate on distributed representations of words, potentially losing information about local syntactic and semantic structures. In this paper, we present the Convolutional Interaction Network (CIN), a novel approach to modeling interactions between sentences in NLI. CIN moves away from the traditional attention paradigm and instead focuses on dynamically generating filters based on one sentence and applying them to encode the other. response: Opinion mining, also known as sentiment analysis, has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its wide range of applications, including market research, brand monitoring, and customer relationship management (Liu, 2012). A crucial subtask within opinion mining is identifying *opinion targets* – the entities or aspects about which opinions are expressed. For instance, in the review "The battery life of this phone is amazing," the opinion target is "battery life." Accurately extracting opinion targets is fundamental to understanding the nuanced sentiments expressed in online reviews and provides valuable insights for businesses and consumers alike. Existing approaches to opinion target extraction broadly fall into two categories: syntax-based methods and alignment-based methods. Syntax-based methods leverage syntactic parsing to identify relationships between opinion words and target entities (Nasukawa & Iguchi, 2005; Zhuang et al., 2006). These methods typically define syntactic patterns – pre-defined structures describing how opinion words modify target entities. For example, a pattern might specify that an adjective expressing sentiment should directly modify a noun, indicating the target. However, a major limitation of these approaches is their reliance on accurate syntactic parsing. Online reviews are often characterized by informal language, grammatical errors, and unconventional sentence structures, making accurate parsing a challenging task, and consequently degrading the performance of syntax-based opinion target extraction (Liddy, 2001). In contrast, alignment-based methods employ word alignment models to identify associations between opinion words and target entities, circumventing the need for explicit syntactic parsing (Wan & Xiao, 2008; Jiang et al., 2013). These models learn statistical relationships between words in a sentence, identifying likely dependencies without relying on a pre-defined grammatical structure. This makes them more robust to the noisy and informal nature of online text. However, alignment-based methods can sometimes struggle to capture complex syntactic relationships that are crucial for accurately identifying opinion targets. Despite the contrasting strengths and weaknesses of these two approaches, there has been limited empirical investigation into which method performs better under varying conditions. Specifically, the influence of corpus size, domain specificity, and language remains largely unexplored. This paper aims to address this gap by conducting a comprehensive comparative study of syntax-based and alignment-based methods for opinion target extraction. Furthermore, motivated by the complementary nature of these approaches, we investigate a novel combination strategy employing a partially supervised framework. We hypothesize that integrating syntactic patterns with alignment models can leverage the strengths of both, mitigating their respective limitations and improving overall performance, particularly in scenarios with limited training data. We evaluate the effectiveness of this combined approach across a variety of experimental settings. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed combination is particularly effective for corpora of small and medium sizes, offering a promising avenue for enhancing opinion target extraction in practical applications. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: * An empirical comparison of syntax-based and alignment-based methods for opinion target extraction across different corpus sizes, domains, and languages. * A novel partially supervised framework for combining syntactic patterns with alignment models. * Experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the combined approach, particularly in low-resource scenarios.

response: Statistical Machine Transliteration (SMT) has emerged as a vital component in numerous cross-lingual Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, particularly those involving proper names, technical terms, and brand names. Unlike traditional machine translation, which focuses on semantic equivalence, transliteration aims to map the *form* of a word from a source language to its corresponding form in a target language, preserving its pronunciation or orthographic similarity. While dictionary-based approaches served as an initial solution, their scalability is limited, requiring substantial manual effort to curate and maintain comprehensive transliteration lexicons. Consequently, research has shifted towards statistical approaches that leverage parallel corpora to automatically learn transliteration mappings. A prevalent paradigm in statistical transliteration involves identifying and aligning phrase pairs that represent transliteration equivalents within bilingual corpora. These phrase pairs act as training data for statistical models, typically based on noisy channel models or alignments learned through Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithms. However, automatically extracted phrase pairs are often riddled with noise – instances where the identified pairs are not true transliterations but rather accidental alignments resulting from data sparsity, incorrect word segmentation, or simply coincidental string similarity. This noise significantly degrades the performance of downstream transliteration models. Existing alignment methods often struggle to differentiate between genuine transliteration pairs and noisy alignments. Traditional many-to-many alignment models, while capturing the inherent complexities of character-level mappings, typically do not explicitly account for the presence of noise. This leads to the incorporation of spurious alignments, diluting the signal from actual transliteration pairs and hindering model generalization. Moreover, bootstrapping transliteration systems often face the “cold start” problem—a lack of initial training data limits the effectiveness of initial alignment, perpetuating a cycle of poor performance. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing a novel noise-aware character alignment method specifically designed for bootstrapping SMT from automatically extracted phrase pairs. Our approach extends a Bayesian many-to-many alignment framework to explicitly model and distinguish non-transliteration parts within phrase pairs, effectively identifying and downweighting noisy alignments. We introduce a probabilistic model that estimates the likelihood of an alignment being a true transliteration versus noise, incorporating features derived from character-level similarity, length differences, and contextual information. By explicitly modeling noise, our method improves the accuracy of character alignment, leading to the identification of more reliable phrase pairs for training the transliteration model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments focused on bootstrapping Japanese-to-English statistical machine transliteration within the specialized domain of patents. Patent data, while plentiful, is characterized by a high degree of technical terminology and often exhibits noisy alignments due to variations in naming conventions and the inherent complexity of technical language. Our results show significant improvements in transliteration performance when utilizing our noise-aware alignment method compared to traditional alignment techniques, illustrating its capability to effectively bootstrap a transliteration system even in the presence of substantial noise. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses related work in statistical machine transliteration and alignment modeling. Section 3 details our proposed noise-aware character alignment method. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work.

response: Recent advances in deep learning have led to significant progress in natural language understanding (NLU) across a wide range of tasks (Young et al., 2018; Howard & Ruder, 2018). However, many existing NLU benchmarks focus on relatively narrow domains or require substantial human annotation, limiting their scalability and generalizability. Furthermore, a growing body of research highlights the importance of reasoning over structured knowledge for robust language understanding (Davis & Marcus, 2015; Zhong et al., 2018). The ability to integrate textual information with structured knowledge representations is crucial for building truly intelligent systems. Wikidata (Krötzsch et al., 2013), a collaboratively edited, multilingual knowledge base, provides a rich source of structured knowledge. Paired with its corresponding Wikipedia articles, it offers an unprecedented opportunity to develop and evaluate NLU models capable of grounding language in real-world facts. In this paper, we introduce WIKIREADING, a novel large-scale language understanding task designed to address these challenges. WIKIREADING consists of 18 million instances, generated by automatically extracting relationships from Wikidata and formulating them as natural language questions requiring information to be retrieved from the corresponding Wikipedia articles. Unlike traditional question answering tasks that often rely on curated datasets with limited scope, WIKIREADING leverages the vast knowledge contained within Wikipedia and Wikidata, enabling the creation of a diverse and challenging benchmark. The task inherently requires models to perform both document-level reading comprehension and knowledge base reasoning, bridging the gap between unstructured text and structured data. The task formulation in WIKIREADING presents a versatile framework encompassing various NLU sub-tasks. Instances can be framed as classification problems (e.g., predicting the type of a relationship), or extraction problems (e.g., identifying the specific textual value corresponding to a Wikidata property). This versatility renders WIKIREADING an ideal platform for evaluating and comparing end-to-end models, such as deep neural networks (DNNs), capable of handling complex reasoning scenarios without relying on hand-engineered features. We conduct extensive experiments comparing a spectrum of state-of-the-art DNN-based architectures, including those commonly employed for document classification, information extraction, and question answering. Our findings demonstrate that models capable of supporting a rich answer space—specifically, word or character sequences—outperform those constrained to discrete options. While these rule-based systems offer substantial control over the generated output, they are brittle, knowledge-intensive, and difficult to scale to new domains or languages. However, achieving robust and accurate sentiment analysis across multiple languages remains a challenging endeavor. A critical, often overlooked, factor influencing language variation is the demographic characteristics of the speaker or writer. Individuals categorized by attributes such as age, gender, socioeconomic status, and geographic location frequently exhibit distinct linguistic patterns, particularly in informal communication channels like social media. These variations extend beyond simple lexical choices, encompassing stylistic preferences, emotional expression, and the use of non-verbal cues like emoticons and hashtags. We hypothesize that systematic differences exist in how men and women express sentiment online, even within the same language, and that accounting for these differences can enhance the performance of multilingual sentiment analysis systems. Our study focuses on three languages – English, Spanish, and Russian – chosen to represent diverse linguistic families and cultural backgrounds. We leverage large-scale Twitter datasets to analyze differences in subjective language, emoticon usage, and hashtag preferences between male and female users. response: The study of poetic meter, or scansion, has long been a cornerstone of literary analysis. Understanding the rhythmic structure of a poem – the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables – provides valuable insight into its aesthetic effect, and often reveals deliberate artistic choices made by the poet. Traditional English poetry frequently adheres to established metrical patterns like iambic pentameter, trochaic tetrameter, and others. However, the reality of poetic practice is rarely so rigid. Skilled poets deliberately introduce variations, substitutions, and even outright deviations from these norms to create nuanced effects, emphasizing certain words or phrases, mirroring emotional shifts, or simply avoiding monotony. This inherent tension between predictable structure and creative license poses a significant challenge to the automation of metrical analysis. Despite the rich history of computational linguistics, automated scansion remains a surprisingly difficult task. Early attempts relied on hand-coded rules and dictionaries of pronunciation, but these systems proved brittle and unable to generalize to diverse poetic styles or handle ambiguous cases (see, for example, work by Nolan, 1994). More recent approaches, leveraging the power of machine learning, offer a promising avenue for addressing these limitations. However, simply training a classifier on annotated data is complicated by the factors previously mentioned: the expected deviations from standard rhythmic patterns, the ambiguity inherent in poetic language, and the subjective nature of scansion itself – even human experts can disagree on the metrical interpretation of certain lines (Hayes & MacPherson, 1983). In this paper, we explore the application of several Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to the problem of automatic scansion of English poetry. Our goal is not to present a definitive solution – indeed, we argue that achieving perfect accuracy is likely an unattainable ideal given the complexities of the task. Rather, we aim to establish a baseline performance using readily available NLP tools and a relatively straightforward machine learning pipeline. We train and evaluate our systems on a newly created, human-annotated corpus of English poetry, carefully selected to represent a range of poetic styles and periods. This corpus will become a valuable resource for future research in this area. Through these experiments, we seek to highlight both the potential and the limitations of current NLP methods for metrical analysis. response: Entity retrieval, the task of identifying entities that satisfy a user’s information need, has become a cornerstone of modern information access. Traditional information retrieval (IR) models often represent documents and queries as bags-of-words, neglecting the rich semantic structure inherent in both. While significant progress has been made with methods incorporating semantic representations like knowledge graphs (Sun et al., 2018) and distributional semantics (Yamada et al., 2020), effectively representing *entities* – and the nuanced ways users seek information *about* entities – remains a substantial challenge. Many entity search systems rely on keyword matching against entity attributes or descriptions. However, this approach suffers from several limitations. Firstly, users are often uncertain about the precise wording to use when formulating their queries (Allan, 2000). Secondly, a single entity can be described by a multitude of facts, and the relevance of these facts varies depending on the user’s intent. For example, a user searching for “actors born in New York” is interested in a specific factoid about actors, rather than a broad description of their filmography or awards. Finally, these systems struggle to leverage the hierarchical relationships between different facets of an entity’s characteristics. We hypothesize that entity queries are not directly formulated with full descriptions, but rather emerge from a two-stage cognitive process. First, a user identifies distinguishing *facts* about the target entity – properties that differentiate it from others. Then, they select words to articulate those facts in a query. Consider a user searching for a ‘jazz musician’. They might implicitly consider facts like ‘plays saxophone’, ‘born in New Orleans’, or ‘associated with bebop’ before settling on a query like ‘saxophone player from New Orleans’. Inspired by this query generation paradigm, we propose a novel entity representation model called the *Entity Factoid Hierarchy* (EFH). The EFH is a tree-structured representation where nodes contain factoids – concise statements describing an entity at varying levels of granularity. This hierarchy allows for capturing not only individual facts but also the relationships between them, mirroring the user’s potential thought process. The construction of the EFH is grounded in a factor graph model, allowing for probabilistic reasoning about factoid relevance. Inference within this factor graph utilizes a modified Multiple-try Metropolis algorithm to efficiently explore the solution space. Entity retrieval is then framed as decomposing the user’s query into its constituent factoids and computing the likelihood of the query given the entity’s factoid hierarchy. We demonstrate through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets that our EFH-based framework significantly outperforms existing entity retrieval models, highlighting the effectiveness of incorporating structured, factoid-based entity representations. This work provides a new perspective on entity retrieval and opens up avenues for developing more intelligent and intuitive entity search systems. Allan, J. (2000). response: The automatic identification of sentiment – the subjective information expressed in text – has become a crucial component of many natural language processing applications, ranging from customer feedback analysis to political polling (Pang and Lee, 2008;Liu, 2012). A fundamental building block for most sentiment analysis systems is a semantic orientation lexicon, which assigns polarity scores (positive, negative, or neutral) to words and phrases. While supervised machine learning approaches can be highly accurate, they necessitate large, manually annotated training corpora, a resource that is often unavailable or costly to create. Consequently, unsupervised or semi-supervised lexicon-based methods remain a popular choice. Existing lexicon creation techniques typically leverage lexical resources like WordNet (Miller, 1995) to expand a seed set of positive and negative words. Methods pioneered by Turney and Littman (2002) and expanded upon by others (Kanayama et al., 2006;Spertus et al., 2005) rely on measuring semantic similarity between words within WordNet’s hierarchical structure. While effective, these approaches often require significant computational resources, particularly when scaling to large vocabularies, and their performance is heavily influenced by the completeness and accuracy of WordNet itself. Furthermore, many rely on large corpora to estimate word co-occurrence statistics, introducing another dependency. In contrast, we propose a novel and strikingly simple method for generating a high-coverage semantic orientation lexicon. Our approach eschews the complexity of WordNet, instead relying on the structured relationships found within a standard Roget-like thesaurus – a resource focusing on conceptual relations rather than lexical definitions – coupled with a small list of overtly sentiment-bearing affixes. This allows us to bootstrap a lexicon quickly and efficiently, covering both single words and multi-word expressions without the need for extensive manual annotation or large-scale corpus analysis. Traditionally, this task has been approached as a “one-shot” problem - generating a single, comprehensive expression intended to uniquely identify a target object within a scene (Dale & Reiter, 1995; Kelleher et al., 2008). However, human communication rarely relies on perfect, upfront specification. Instead, we frequently engage in iterative refinement, offering referring information in “installments” and soliciting feedback to ensure mutual understanding. For example, instead of saying “the large red mug on the left,” one might start with “the mug…” and then add details like “the red one” or “the large one” based on the listener’s response. This incremental approach allows for error correction, clarification of ambiguities, and adaptation to the listener’s knowledge state. This paper explores the benefits of adopting an installment-based strategy for REG in technical systems. We argue that such an approach is particularly advantageous when the system operates with imperfect information – for instance, when object recognition is uncertain or attribute classification is unreliable. In these scenarios, attempting a single, highly specific expression upfront may lead to the inclusion of incorrect details, hindering rather than aiding successful reference. Unlike traditional relation extraction, which focuses on pre-defined relations and requires labeled data, OIE aims to extract relations in a fully unsupervised and domain-independent manner. This capability is crucial for building large-scale knowledge bases and enabling various downstream applications, such as question answering, knowledge discovery, and text summarization. First, they tend to generate a large volume of noisy and redundant extractions, hindering their usability (Finkelstein et al., 2010). Many extractions contain unnecessary details or are overly specific, leading to diminished utility and increased storage costs. Second, crucial semantic information, such as polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities, is often embedded directly within the extracted relation phrase, making it difficult to analyze and reason with the extracted knowledge. MinIE operates under the principle of “minimizing facts,” aiming to extract only the essential information while representing auxiliary details through structured semantic annotations. Our work contributes to the advancement of OIE by promoting the extraction of high-quality, compact facts that are readily usable for downstream applications. response: The field of grounded language learning (GLL) aims to bridge the gap between language understanding and real-world interaction. A central challenge within GLL is enabling agents to interpret and execute natural language instructions within a simulated or real-world environment. This necessitates not merely understanding the linguistic content, but crucially, mapping that understanding to appropriate actions within that environment. Recent approaches have focused on tasks such as robotic manipulation (Tellex et al., 2011), visual dialog (Dasgupta et al., 2018), and, notably, navigation (Hermann et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019). The task of learning to follow navigation instructions, where an agent must interpret commands like “Turn left at the next corner” and translate them into a sequence of actions, presents a particularly compelling benchmark for GLL. Such tasks require compositional understanding – breaking down complex instructions into elementary steps – and robust generalization to novel environments and instructions. A common paradigm for tackling this challenge involves a two-stage process: first, generating a set of candidate action sequences (often referred to as “plans” or “trajectories”) based on the language input and environmental observations; and second, selecting the most appropriate candidate from this set. Initial approaches relied heavily on rule-based systems or hand-engineered features (Chen & Schuler, 2013). More recently, sequence-to-sequence models (Sutskever et al., 2014) and reinforcement learning (Mnih et al., 2015) have demonstrated promising results. However, a key limitation of these end-to-end approaches is their susceptibility to error propagation – a single incorrect prediction early in the sequence can derail the entire plan. In contrast, discriminative reranking offers a powerful mechanism for refining the output of a generative model. Originally developed for syntactic and semantic parsing (Collins, 2009), reranking leverages a discriminative model to score and reorder a set of candidate parses, typically trained on gold-standard parse trees. This allows the reranker to correct errors made by the initial generator, leveraging richer features and global context. However, directly applying this paradigm to GLL poses a significant challenge: unlike traditional parsing tasks, obtaining gold-standard “parse trees” – representing the optimal sequence of actions – is often impractical or impossible in a grounded setting. Annotating such data is costly, time-consuming, and requires expert knowledge of the environment. This paper investigates the adaptation of discriminative reranking techniques to the grounded language acquisition task of navigation instruction following. We propose a novel approach that circumvents the need for gold-standard reference trajectories by utilizing weak supervision from task completion feedback. Specifically, we train the reranker to prefer action sequences that lead to successful task completion (reaching the specified goal) over those that do not. We demonstrate, through comprehensive experiments, that this approach achieves performance comparable to training on fully supervised gold-standard trajectories, offering a viable and scalable alternative for improving grounded language acquisition systems. Our contribution lies in demonstrating the effectiveness of leveraging implicit feedback as a substitute for explicit supervision in the context of discriminative reranking for GLL.

response: The ability for robots to understand and execute human instructions is a cornerstone of truly assistive robotics. While significant progress has been made in robot locomotion and perception, a persistent challenge remains in bridging the semantic gap between natural language commands and the low-level control signals required for robot action. For a robot to operate effectively in human environments, it must not only perceive its surroundings but also interpret ambiguous, high-level instructions like “Go to the kitchen and then turn left at the counter” or “Find the office with the blue door.” Traditional robotics approaches often rely on hand-engineered rules and carefully defined state spaces, proving brittle and difficult to scale to complex, real-world scenarios. More recently, the rise of deep learning has offered promising avenues for tackling this problem, enabling robots to learn directly from data without explicit programming. However, several key challenges persist in natural language instruction following. Firstly, natural language is inherently ambiguous and context-dependent. The meaning of "the counter" depends on the specific environment, necessitating a system capable of grounding language in the robot’s perceptual experience. Secondly, effectively planning a robot’s behavior requires reasoning about the environment’s structure and constraints. A simple sequence of actions, such as “go forward, turn left,” may be insufficient for navigating complex spaces with obstacles or multiple potential paths. Finally, many existing approaches focus on directly predicting low-level actions, limiting the robot’s ability to generalize to new situations or to adapt its plan based on unforeseen circumstances. In this work, we address these challenges by proposing an end-to-end deep learning model for translating free-form natural language instructions into a *high-level plan* for behavioral robot navigation (Figure 1). We employ attention mechanisms to dynamically connect relevant information from the user instruction with specific nodes in the topological map. response: Activity recognition has become a central problem in computer vision, with applications ranging from human-robot interaction to video surveillance. Traditional approaches to activity recognition rely on supervised learning, requiring extensive labeled training data for each activity of interest. However, obtaining such datasets is costly and time-consuming, particularly when dealing with the long tail of human actions. This limitation motivates the development of zero-shot activity recognition (ZSL) techniques, which aim to recognize activities not seen during training. Recent advances in ZSL leverage semantic information to bridge the gap between seen and unseen classes. A common paradigm involves projecting both visual features and semantic representations into a shared embedding space, enabling the recognition of unseen activities based on their semantic descriptions (Socher et al., 2013;Farhadi et al., 2014;Romera-Paredes and Torr, 2015). Much of the existing work in ZSL focuses on utilizing object attributes—descriptive properties of the objects involved in an action (e.g., a "ball" is "round" and "bouncy"). For example, recognizing the activity "throwing a ball" might rely on identifying a hand, a ball, and understanding the attributes of a ball. However, this approach can be limited, as many activities are defined more accurately by the *action* itself, rather than the objects involved. Consider the activity "salute"; while a hand is involved, the defining characteristic is the manner of movement and the social context. Furthermore, many prior approaches assume access to hand-annotated attributes for both seen and unseen classes. This reliance on gold-standard attributes introduces a new bottleneck, as annotating attributes is itself a laborious task. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to zero-shot activity recognition that directly models the visual and linguistic attributes of *action verbs*, rather than objects. We validate our approach on a challenging activity recognition benchmark, demonstrating significant improvements over existing techniques.

response: Search queries represent a unique and increasingly important form of human-computer interaction. Unlike traditional text, search queries are typically short, often ungrammatical, and exhibit a distinctive style reflecting users’ information needs and interaction with search engines (Jansen et al., 2008;Spink et al., 2002). Consequently, accurately processing and understanding search queries is crucial for building effective information retrieval (IR) systems. A key component of query understanding is linguistic annotation – assigning tags denoting part-of-speech (POS), capitalization patterns, segmentation into multi-word expressions, and other relevant features. These annotations facilitate tasks such as query expansion, query suggestion, and relevance ranking. However, annotating search queries poses significant challenges. The brevity of queries often leads to ambiguity, making it difficult for standard Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools – typically trained on well-formed text – to perform accurately (Han et al., 2010). Furthermore, the informal and idiosyncratic nature of query language, including the frequent use of abbreviations, misspellings, and non-standard phrasing, exacerbates these difficulties. Existing approaches often rely on adapting general-purpose NLP tools to the query domain, but these adaptations frequently struggle to achieve satisfactory performance (Li et al., 2009). Supervised learning approaches, while potentially accurate, require substantial amounts of labeled query data, which is expensive and time-consuming to obtain. To address these challenges, we propose a novel probabilistic approach for *joint* query annotation. Our method leverages the strengths of both unsupervised and supervised learning techniques, aiming to maximize annotation accuracy even with limited labeled training data. Unlike previous work that typically annotates queries with a single, independent classifier for each tag (e.g., POS tagging, capitalization detection), we adopt a hierarchical framework that explicitly models dependencies between different annotation layers. Our approach begins with deriving a robust set of initial, independent annotations using unsupervised techniques applied to a large corpus of search queries and leveraging pseudo-relevance feedback. These initial annotations form the foundation for subsequent supervised learning. We then stack additional classifiers on top of these initial annotations, specifically designed to exploit the inherent relationships between different annotation types. For instance, the capitalization of a word may strongly influence its predicted POS tag, and correctly identifying multi-word expressions can improve both POS tagging and named entity recognition. By modeling these dependencies, we significantly improve the overall annotation accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our joint annotation approach, consistently outperforming baseline methods and demonstrating significant improvements, particularly when only a limited amount of labeled training data is available. This work contributes a practical and effective solution for accurately annotating search queries, which can directly benefit a wide range of IR applications. In the context of Information Retrieval (IR), this often translates to adapting ranking models trained on large, labeled datasets (e.g., web search logs) to new scenarios where labeled data is limited or unavailable. A common scenario is domain adaptation, where the distribution of queries and documents differs between the source and target domains. For example, a ranking model trained on general web queries might perform poorly on specialized domains like medical literature or scientific publications. Documents from the source domain that are deemed similar to documents in the target domain receive higher weights, effectively biasing the model towards the target distribution. Queries, as representations of user information needs, often exhibit stronger domain-specific characteristics than individual documents. response: The automatic identification of opinions expressed in text is a core task in sentiment analysis and opinion mining, with applications ranging from market research to political monitoring. A crucial component of this task is not simply determining *what* opinions are expressed, but also *who* holds them (the source) and *what* they are about (the target). A particularly effective paradigm, spearheaded by Yang and Cardie (2013), utilizes Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) integrated with Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) for joint inference. This approach achieves strong performance by leveraging a rich set of features derived from lexicons, parsers, and other external knowledge sources. However, the reliance on hand-crafted features and complex preprocessing pipelines represents a significant bottleneck. Maintaining and adapting these features to new domains or languages is a laborious and time-consuming process. LSTMs are capable of learning complex sequential dependencies directly from raw text, potentially alleviating the need for extensive feature engineering. They have demonstrated strong performance in tasks like sequence tagging and sentiment classification. Consequently, the application of LSTMs to joint opinion entity and relation extraction is a natural and compelling direction. response: Semantic relation classification (SRC) is a fundamental task in natural language processing, aiming to identify the semantic relationship between two entities mentioned in a sentence. Identifying these relationships is crucial for a variety of downstream applications, including information extraction, knowledge base population, and question answering. Despite significant progress in recent years, achieving high accuracy in SRC remains a considerable challenge. Traditional approaches to SRC heavily rely on hand-crafted features, such as syntactic parse trees, word embeddings, and lexical patterns (Zeng et al., 2008; Miwa & Saigo, 2010). While these features can be informative, their design requires substantial domain expertise and linguistic knowledge. Moreover, feature engineering can be time-consuming and may not generalize well across different datasets. In recent years, deep learning models have emerged as a promising alternative to traditional feature-based approaches. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (Kim et al., 2014) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) (Socher et al., 2013) have been successfully applied to SRC, demonstrating their ability to automatically learn relevant features from raw text. However, existing deep learning models often struggle to capture the complex contextual information surrounding the target entities. A single RNN, for example, may not effectively encode the different aspects of the sentence relevant to the relationship between the two entities. Furthermore, traditional RNNs treat all words in the sentence equally, potentially overlooking critical information that is most indicative of the underlying relation. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel hierarchical recurrent neural network (HRNN) with attention mechanisms for SRC. Our model is designed to selectively focus on important contextual information and capture the semantic composition of the sentence in a more nuanced manner. The core idea behind our approach is to divide the input sentence into three context subsequences based on the positions of the two entities involved in the relation. Then, a second-level RNN combines these representations to form a unified sentence representation, suitable for relation classification. Crucially, we incorporate attention mechanisms within both RNN layers. This highlights the effectiveness of our hierarchical architecture and attention mechanisms in learning robust and informative sentence representations for semantic relation classification. response: Persuasion is a fundamental aspect of human communication, manifesting in scenarios ranging from everyday negotiations to critical decision-making processes. Recent advances in dialogue systems have begun to explore the potential of automated persuasion, aiming to build agents capable of influencing user beliefs or behaviors through natural language interaction. However, crafting effective persuasive strategies remains a significant challenge. Humans frequently employ sophisticated techniques, such as *framing* – presenting information to emphasize certain aspects and evoke specific emotional responses – to sway their interlocutors. This paper investigates the use of reinforcement learning (RL) to automatically learn cooperative persuasive dialogue policies that leverage framing techniques. Traditional approaches to dialogue system development often rely on hand-crafted rules or supervised learning from manually annotated data. These methods can be labor-intensive and may struggle to generalize to novel situations or adapt to diverse user preferences. Reinforcement learning, on the other hand, offers a promising alternative by allowing agents to learn optimal policies through trial and error, maximizing a reward signal based on their interactions with an environment. Applying RL to persuasive dialogue, however, presents unique difficulties. Constructing a suitable environment, particularly a realistic user model, and defining a reward function that accurately reflects the goals of persuasive interaction are non-trivial tasks. This work addresses these challenges by introducing a novel approach to building user simulators and reward functions specifically tailored for persuasive dialogue. We leverage a corpus of human-human persuasive dialogues to learn patterns of user behavior and to identify key indicators of success in persuasive interactions. These insights inform the design of a user simulator that can realistically respond to different dialogue strategies, and the formulation of a reward function that incentivizes the agent to achieve its persuasive goals while maintaining a cooperative and engaging interaction. Furthermore, we rigorously evaluate the learned policy and the efficacy of framing through a series of experiments. First, we assess the policy’s performance within the simulated environment, providing a controlled setting for analyzing the impact of different framing techniques. Secondly, and crucially, we validate the learned policy with real users through a user study, demonstrating its ability to effectively persuade human interlocutors in practical scenarios. Our results demonstrate that reinforcement learning is a powerful tool for constructing cooperative persuasive dialogue systems capable of utilizing framing strategies to achieve persuasive outcomes, exceeding the performance of baseline approaches and highlighting the potential for creating engaging and effective persuasive agents. It is important to note that our focus is on *cooperative* persuasion; we aim to build agents that respect user autonomy and engage in honest dialogue, rather than employing deceptive or manipulative tactics. This ethical consideration is central to our research and informs the design of our reward function and evaluation methodology.

Currently, evaluation is frequently dominated by n-gram overlap-based metrics like BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and ROUGE (Lin, 2004). response: Question answering (QA) has rapidly advanced with the rise of large knowledge graphs (KGs) like Wikidata and Freebase, and the proliferation of techniques for embedding entities and relations. However, a major bottleneck remains: answering *compositional* questions. These questions require reasoning over multiple relations, applying logical operators (e.g., conjunction, negation, disjunction), and generally performing multi-step inference to arrive at the correct answer. Traditional approaches often struggle with the combinatorial explosion of possible interpretations inherent in compositional queries. Early systems relied on hand-crafted rules and semantic parsing (Zettlemoyer & Collins, 2005; Kwiatkowski et al., 2013), which are brittle, require significant expert knowledge, and don’t scale effectively to complex queries or new knowledge graphs. More recently, neural approaches have shown promise, utilizing recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (Bordes et al., 2015) and their tree-based variants (Tai et al., 2015) to encode questions. However, these models often fall short when faced with longer, more complex questions, or questions that require precise compositional reasoning – largely because they lack an explicit mechanism for representing and manipulating the underlying *meaning* of the question. A key challenge is capturing the semantic structure of a question, and how its constituent parts combine to form a complete denotation. Formal semantics provides a powerful framework for addressing this challenge. Denotational semantics maps linguistic expressions to their underlying meanings, typically defined in terms of mathematical objects. Compositionality dictates that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the rules for combining those meanings. Inspired by these principles, we introduce a novel, end-to-end differentiable model for QA that directly implements a form of neural compositional denotational semantics. Our model represents spans of text not only with a grounded entity set within the KG, but also with a vector that captures potentially *ungrounded* aspects of meaning - representing concepts or operators that don't directly correspond to KG entities. Crucially, we learn learned composition modules that recursively combine these span representations, mirroring the compositional principles of formal semantics. Using the example of a negated phrase like "not green," our model represents "green" as a set of entities and "not" as a learnable vector, leveraging this vector to parameterize a composition function that performs a complement operation, enabling it to reason about entities *not* possessing the "green" property. Unlike semantic parsing approaches that produce a discrete, symbolic parse tree, our model jointly learns both the composition operators and the output structure via gradient descent, directly optimizing for the end task of question answering. By constructing a parse chart subsuming all possible parses for a given question, we enable the model to explore various semantic interpretations simultaneously. This approach allows the model to discover latent syntactic structure and learn surprisingly robust semantic operators, including quantifiers, disjunctions, and composed relations. We demonstrate that our approach not only achieves state-of-the-art performance on several challenging QA datasets but also generalizes effectively to questions longer than those encountered during training, surpassing the performance of RNN, tree-based RNN, and semantic parsing baselines.

However, existing datasets often focus on relatively limited domains, such as airline travel or geographic locations within a specific city. Furthermore, adapting these systems to new domains or languages often requires substantial manual effort in terms of data annotation and model retraining. OpenStreetMap (OSM) presents a particularly compelling, yet challenging, target for natural language querying. As a collaborative, open-source mapping project, OSM contains a wealth of geographic information about the world, ranging from roads and buildings to points of interest and pedestrian pathways. The sheer scale and dynamic nature of OSM, combined with the inherent ambiguity and flexibility of natural language, demand robust and adaptable semantic parsing techniques. Existing work has explored limited aspects of querying OSM with natural language, often relying on keyword-based search or predefined templates (e.g., overpass API queries). However, these approaches struggle to handle the nuances of natural language, such as fuzzy spatial relations (e.g., "nearby,” “close to”) and compositional queries. response: Distributional semantics (DS) has emerged as a dominant paradigm in computational linguistics over the past two decades, offering a compelling approach to representing word meaning based on usage patterns in large text corpora (Lenci et al., 2007; Turney & Pantel, 2010). The core tenet of DS is that “you shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth, 1957), meaning that the semantic properties of a word are reflected in the contexts in which it appears. This principle has led to the development of numerous algorithms – including Latent Semantic Analysis (Deerwester et al., 1990), Hyperspace Analogue to Language (Kanerva et al., 1998), and word embeddings like Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) – that successfully map words to vector representations in a high-dimensional space, capturing semantic similarities and relationships. However, despite the success of DS in representing individual word meanings, a significant challenge remains: extending these representations to encompass the meaning of larger linguistic units, such as phrases and sentences. While some discourse relations are explicitly signaled by discourse connectives (e.g., “because,” “however”), a significant portion remain *implicit*, requiring inference based on contextual cues and world knowledge. Recognizing these implicit discourse relations is a crucial step towards deeper text understanding, enabling applications such as improved machine reading comprehension, text summarization, and question answering. Despite considerable progress in recent years, accurately identifying implicit discourse relations remains a challenging task. Early approaches to discourse relation classification relied heavily on hand-engineered features, capturing lexical, syntactic, and semantic information about the discourse arguments (e.g., the segments of text connected by the relation). While achieving reasonable performance, these systems were often brittle and required significant domain expertise to adapt to new text types. More recently, neural network models have emerged as a dominant paradigm, offering the ability to learn complex features automatically from data. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been successfully applied to this task, often leveraging attention mechanisms to focus on the most relevant parts of the input arguments (e.g., Li et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2017). However, existing neural models often treat discourse relation recognition as a single-pass process – the input is encoded, features are extracted, and a classification decision is made. We argue that this approach overlooks a crucial aspect of human discourse processing: *repeated reading*. When encountering ambiguous or complex text, humans do not typically grasp the relationships between segments in a single pass. Instead, we repeatedly reread the text, gradually refining our understanding and focusing on key signals that help resolve the discourse structure. This iterative process allows us to dynamically identify the most salient features for determining the underlying relation. This work contributes a novel perspective on discourse relation recognition, highlighting the importance of modeling the iterative nature of human comprehension and offering a powerful new approach for tackling this challenging task. Characterized by misspellings, abbreviations, slang, and grammatical errors, social media text poses a significant hurdle for traditional NLP tools, which are typically designed to process well-formed, standard language (Eisenstein, 2013; Han et al., 2013). Dictionary-based methods (Liu et al., 2012; Awad et al., 2013) rely on manually or automatically constructed mappings between non-standard and standard words. While straightforward, these approaches often suffer from limited coverage and struggle to generalize to unseen variations. Learning-based methods, on the other hand, employ machine learning techniques to learn normalization rules from labeled data (Bahasa and Wilks, 2014; Kulkarni et al., 2015). These methods offer better generalization capabilities but require substantial labeled training data, which can be expensive and time-consuming to acquire, particularly for rapidly evolving social media language. Our approach moves beyond relying solely on lexical similarity and incorporates a graph-based representation of the textual data. The task involves identifying and suggesting corrections for misspelled words within a user’s query, aiming to bridge the gap between the user’s intent and the content available on the web. Early approaches to query spelling correction relied heavily on generative models, particularly noisy channel models (Bilmes & Kirchhoff, 2000; Jones & Norvig, 1993). These models estimate the probability of a misspelling given the correct word (the “channel”) and the probability of the correct word itself. While effective, noisy channel models often struggle to capture the complex dependencies between words and the broader context of a query. Recent research has shifted towards a two-stage paradigm (Cai et al., 2010; Jones & Curran, 2009). The first stage employs a noisy channel model to generate a set of candidate corrections for each misspelled word. This is followed by a discriminatively trained ranker, typically a machine learning model, to re-rank these candidates based on various features, ultimately selecting the most likely correct spelling. This approach leverages the strengths of both generative and discriminative modeling. However, this seemingly advantageous combination presents a significant challenge: the performance of the discriminative ranker is fundamentally limited by the quality – specifically, the recall – of the candidate set generated by the initial noisy channel model. If the noisy channel model fails to propose the correct spelling as a candidate, the subsequent ranking stage has no opportunity to select it, leading to a suboptimal correction. Our model, a Latent Structural Support Vector Machine (SVM), directly models the mapping from misspelled queries to correct queries, without relying on an explicit candidate generation step. We argue that by learning a direct discriminative function, we can overcome the recall bottleneck inherent in the two-stage approach and achieve significantly improved correction accuracy. These models, often realized as finite-state tree transducers (FSTs), learn to map syntactic structures from a source to a target language, capturing sophisticated relationships beyond simple string-based substitutions. However, successfully building such transducers relies heavily on two key components: accurate word alignments and an effective rule extraction algorithm. Traditional rule extraction methods typically leverage word alignments as a starting point, identifying corresponding phrases and constructing transduction rules based on these correspondences (Knight and Graehl, 1997; Vogel et al., 2003). These alignments effectively serve as anchors, guiding the induction of grammatical rules. However, this alignment-driven approach suffers from a critical limitation, particularly in scenarios characterized by limited training data. When the size of the corpus of paired trees/strings is small relative to the vocabulary size or the complexity of the targeted grammar, the resulting word alignments become unreliable and often contain significant noise (Och and Ney, 2003). This unreliability then cascades through the rule extraction process, leading to the induction of spurious or overly generalized rules, ultimately hindering the transducer's performance. Consider, for example, attempting to build a tree transducer for mapping question structures to their corresponding SQL queries from a small set of question-query pairs. The inherent ambiguity in natural language and the limited data can easily result in inaccurate alignments, leading to a transducer that fails to generalize beyond the training examples. To address these limitations, we propose a novel rule extraction algorithm that minimizes reliance on pre-computed word alignments. Instead, our approach directly optimizes a cost function over tree fragments, formulating rule extraction as a cost minimization problem. This allows the algorithm to identify potentially valuable transduction rules based directly on the structure and content of the training data, independent of potentially noisy alignments. Furthermore, and perhaps more importantly, our formulation naturally lends itself to a dynamic rule creation process. This challenge lies at the heart of achieving truly *deep* language understanding - moving beyond syntactic parsing and semantic role labeling to capture the rich web of commonsense knowledge that humans implicitly employ when interpreting narratives. A crucial component of this commonsense knowledge involves understanding the causal and correlational relationships between events: knowing, for example, that dropping a glass often *causes* it to break, or that going to a restaurant is frequently *followed by* receiving a bill. Despite considerable interest within the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, progress in modeling and learning these commonsense relationships has been notably hampered by a lack of robust and targeted evaluation frameworks. Existing benchmarks often focus on isolated fact verification or limited forms of reasoning, failing to capture the nuanced, sequential understanding required to comprehend a full narrative. Consequently, it's difficult to definitively assess whether progress in story understanding is driven by genuine commonsense reasoning or simply by exploiting superficial statistical patterns in the data. This paper addresses this critical gap by introducing a new evaluation paradigm – the “Story Cloze Test” – specifically designed to probe deeper understanding of commonsense stories. The task requires a system to select the most plausible concluding sentence from a set of options, given a four-sentence story as context. response: Dialogue is a fundamentally cooperative activity (Grice, 1975). Participants generally assume that their interlocutors are attempting to communicate meaningfully and adhere to a set of implicit conversational principles, often characterized as maxims of quantity, quality, relation, and manner. However, real-world dialogues frequently exhibit instances of non-cooperation, where one or more participants deviate from these norms. Understanding and modeling non-cooperation is crucial for developing robust and intelligent dialogue systems, as well as for analyzing natural language interactions in diverse contexts. Existing approaches to identifying non-cooperation fall into several broad categories. One line of research focuses on *task-related* non-cooperation, where a participant actively hinders the successful completion of a shared goal (e.g., Trappl et al., 2008). This often manifests in behaviors such as providing misleading information or refusing to answer questions directly. Another approach involves defining specific rules or patterns that characterize non-cooperative acts (e.g., a refusal to answer is explicitly labeled as a non-cooperative behavior), requiring expert annotation and often being domain-specific (e.g., Carberry, 1990; Clark & Brennan, 1991). These rule-based methods often struggle to generalize beyond the scenarios for which they were designed and can be brittle in the face of subtle variations in linguistic expression. A key limitation of previous work is that it frequently defines non-cooperation *directly*, rather than measuring it *relative* to an established baseline of cooperative behavior. This paper departs from these approaches by proposing a novel method for quantifying non-cooperation based on the degree to which participants adhere to conventions governing proper dialogue conduct. The model is evaluated on a corpus of political interviews, where levels of cooperation and confrontation are naturally varied. The results demonstrate that our model can accurately predict the degree of cooperation for the interviewer role and reliably assess the relative cooperation levels of both dialogue participants. This work opens up new opportunities for analyzing natural language interactions and building more sophisticated dialogue systems capable of recognizing and responding to subtle cues of non-cooperation.

With the increasing prevalence of online learning platforms and large-scale assessments, the demand for robust and accurate AES systems has grown significantly. Current state-of-the-art AES systems, often leveraging techniques from Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML), can achieve remarkable correlations with human raters (Burstein et al., 2013; Shermis & Burstein, 2013). The challenge is particularly acute when deploying AES systems across diverse educational contexts. The content and style of essays vary considerably depending on the specific prompt or task presented to students. Consequently, an AES model trained on essays from one prompt often exhibits a significant performance degradation when applied to essays generated in response to a different prompt (Landauer et al., 1998). This phenomenon, known as *domain shift*, highlights the need for techniques that can generalize AES models to unseen prompts without requiring extensive new labeled data. The traditional approach to addressing this problem involves collecting and annotating a large corpus of essays for each new prompt, which is both time-consuming and financially prohibitive. Domain adaptation offers a more pragmatic solution by transferring knowledge learned from a source domain (an existing prompt with ample labeled data) to a target domain (a new prompt with limited or no labeled data). Various domain adaptation techniques have been explored in AES, including feature-based approaches (e.g., transforming essay representations to reduce domain divergence) and instance-based approaches (e.g., re-weighting training instances to emphasize those most relevant to the target domain). We hypothesize that the underlying scoring functions for different prompts, while varying in their specific parameters, share a common statistical structure. By modeling the correlations between the scoring functions, our method can adapt the source model to the target domain with minimal labeled data requirements. We evaluate our proposed technique on the publicly available Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) dataset, a widely used benchmark for AES research. Our experimental results demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms several established domain adaptation algorithms, establishing it as a competitive default choice for AES tasks requiring generalization across prompts. The key contributions of this work include a novel domain adaptation framework for AES, a practical implementation based on correlated linear regression, and a comprehensive evaluation demonstrating its effectiveness on a real-world dataset. response: Named Entity Recognition (NER), the task of identifying and classifying named entities in text, is a fundamental component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. In recent years, statistical machine learning models, particularly those employing sequence labeling techniques like Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) and increasingly, deep neural networks, have achieved state-of-the-art performance in NER (Lample et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2015). A key strength of these models lies in their ability to generalize to unseen entities – recognizing entities not explicitly observed during training – by leveraging rich lexical and contextual features. However, despite these advancements, NER systems remain vulnerable to errors, particularly when faced with ambiguous entity mentions or when features incorrectly favor a suboptimal entity type assignment. For instance, the mention “Apple” could refer to the technology company or the fruit. Without sufficient disambiguating context, a model might incorrectly classify it based on spurious feature correlations. This issue is exacerbated in multilingual settings, where the availability of large, high-quality labeled training data is often limited, and the nuances of entity typing can vary significantly across languages. While cross-lingual transfer learning and multilingual embeddings offer some mitigation, they often don’t fully address the fundamental problem of accurate entity type disambiguation. To tackle this challenge, we explore the potential of leveraging Wikipedia, a vast and readily available open knowledge base, to enhance multilingual NER systems. Wikipedia provides a wealth of structured information about entities, including their types (e.g., “Person”, “Organization”, “Location”). Our core contribution is the creation of high-accuracy, high-coverage multilingual Wikipedia entity type mappings. These mappings link entity mentions across multiple languages to their corresponding Wikipedia entries and, crucially, to their associated entity types. Importantly, our method for building these mappings relies on weakly supervised techniques, minimizing the need for costly and time-consuming human annotation. Furthermore, our approach is designed to be easily extended to new languages without requiring language-specific knowledge or expertise. Building upon these mappings, we develop several strategies for integrating Wikipedia-derived information into an existing NER pipeline. We hypothesize that enriching the feature set with knowledge of an entity’s Wikipedia type can significantly improve NER accuracy, particularly for unseen entities and in low-resource scenarios. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed approaches through comprehensive experiments on NER systems trained for six different languages. The results demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements in F1 score, particularly in discerning entity types for novel entities and when training data is scarce—yielding improvements of up to 18.3 F1 points. This work highlights the power of combining statistical machine learning with structured knowledge resources for more robust and accurate multilingual NER. It has become an increasingly important problem in natural language processing with numerous applications, including document indexing, information retrieval, and text summarization. Traditional approaches to KPG typically fall into two main categories: extraction-based and generation-based. Extraction-based methods identify and rank existing phrases within the document based on statistical features or graph-based algorithms (e.g., TextRank; Mihalcea & Tarau, 2004). While computationally efficient, these methods are limited by the vocabulary present in the source document and may fail to capture abstractive concepts. In contrast, generation-based methods, also known as abstractive keyphrase generation, aim to generate novel keyphrases that may not explicitly appear in the document, offering more flexibility and potentially better coverage of the document's content (Meng et al., 2017). Recent advances in sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models with attention mechanisms have demonstrated promising results in abstractive KPG (Rush et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017). These models typically treat KPG as a multi-label classification problem, where the model predicts a sequence of keyphrases given an input document. However, many existing seq2seq models suffer from limitations that hinder the quality of generated keyphrases. A prominent issue is the tendency to generate redundant or overlapping keyphrases.
