response: Graphical models provide a powerful framework for representing and reasoning about complex probabilistic systems. However, exact inference in these models is often intractable, necessitating the use of approximate inference techniques. Variational inference and belief propagation (BP) are two prominent approaches, each with its strengths and weaknesses. Belief propagation, in particular, enjoys widespread use due to its conceptual simplicity and efficiency, but its performance degrades significantly on graphs with loops (loopy graphs). Expectation propagation (EP) offers an improvement over standard BP by maintaining tractable message approximations through a series of local projections (Minka, 2001). In essence, EP iteratively refines approximate factors in the model by matching moments with the true posterior distribution, effectively propagating information between variables. While EP often outperforms BP, its computational cost can still be substantial, particularly when dealing with complex factorizations or high-dimensional variables. Moreover, the resulting messages can sometimes be overly complex, hindering both computational efficiency and interpretability. This paper introduces Penalized Expectation Propagation (PEP), a novel algorithm designed to address these limitations. PEP builds upon the foundation of EP by incorporating a structured-sparsity penalty into the message approximation process. This penalty encourages simpler messages, reducing computational burden and promoting generalization. By carefully balancing the accuracy of the moment matching with the complexity of the resulting messages, PEP aims to achieve a favorable trade-off between speed and accuracy. A key contribution of this work lies in the specific instantiation of PEP for graphical models over strings. String-valued random variables are ubiquitous in natural language processing, computational linguistics, and bioinformatics. Representing and reasoning about these variables often requires sophisticated probabilistic models capable of capturing sequential dependencies. We adaptively approximate finite-state distributions, a common choice for string modeling, by leveraging variable-order n-gram models within the PEP framework. This allows us to efficiently represent long-range dependencies while maintaining tractability. We evaluate the performance of PEP on a series of phonological inference problems. These tasks, which involve reasoning about the underlying sound structure of words, provide a challenging testbed for probabilistic inference algorithms. Our experimental results demonstrate substantial speedups over previous state-of-the-art algorithms, including related approaches based on expectation propagation and variational inference, with no significant loss in accuracy. These findings highlight the effectiveness of PEP in balancing computational efficiency and accuracy for graphical models over strings. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a brief overview of expectation propagation. Section 3 details the formulation of penalized expectation propagation and the specific implementation of the structured-sparsity penalty. Section 4 presents the application of PEP to graphical models over strings using variable-order n-gram approximations. Section 5 describes our experimental setup and reports our results. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and discusses avenues for future research. References: Minka, T. P. (2001). Expectation propagation as a generalization of generalized linear models. *Bayesian statistics*, *6*, 353–364.

response: Relation Extraction (RE) – the task of identifying semantic relationships between entities in text – is a core component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including knowledge base completion, question answering, and information retrieval (Zettlemoyer & Collins, 2005; Mintz et al., 2009; Richardson et al., 2013). Traditionally, building high-performing RE systems required large amounts of manually annotated training data, a process that is both expensive and time-consuming. Distant Supervision (DS) emerged as a promising alternative (Mintz et al., 2009), leveraging existing knowledge bases (KBs) to automatically generate training instances. The core idea is to align entities mentioned in text with entities in the KB and assume that sentences mentioning related entities express the corresponding relation. However, DS is inherently noisy. The assumption that any sentence aligning with a KB relation expresses that relation is often incorrect. These errors arise from various sources, including relation ambiguity (a single sentence can express multiple relations), incorrect KB entries, and implicit relations not explicitly stated in the text. This noise can significantly degrade the performance of RE models trained with DS data, diminishing the benefits of reduced labeling effort. Recent research has focused on addressing the noise issue in DS-RE. Several approaches have been proposed, including multi-instance learning (Riedel et al., 2013), selective instance learning (Hoffmann et al., 2016), and attention mechanisms (Lin et al., 2016). These methods aim to identify and mitigate the impact of noisy instances, but often rely on heuristics or auxiliary information to estimate instance labels. In this work, we argue that the noise in DS-RE can be effectively characterized by a *dynamic transition matrix*. This matrix represents the probability of transitioning between different relation types in the training data. By learning this matrix, we can capture the patterns of noisy instances and leverage this understanding to improve relation extraction performance. Unlike previous methods that treat noise as a static property, our approach recognizes that the noise level and patterns vary depending on the relation type and the context of the sentence. We propose a novel curriculum learning-based method to effectively train the dynamic transition matrix *without any direct supervision about the noise*. The curriculum learning strategy gradually increases the difficulty of the training instances, allowing the model to learn the transition matrix in a stable and efficient manner. We evaluate our approach extensively on a variety of RE datasets and demonstrate that it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of our dynamic transition matrix and curriculum learning strategy in enhancing DS-RE performance. Our contributions lie in a novel characterization of noise in distant supervision, coupled with a novel training scheme to learn that noise effectively, leading to significant improvements in relation extraction. Further, we publicly release our code and trained models to foster future research in this area.

While significant research has been dedicated to assessing and improving readability in languages like English (Flesch, 1954; Dale & Chall, 1948), the study of readability in other languages, particularly those with complex linguistic structures like Bangla, remains relatively underexplored. Bangla, spoken by over 265 million people worldwide, presents unique challenges to computational readability assessment due to its morphological richness, complex sentence structures, and a writing system that differs significantly from Latin-based scripts. Existing readability measures developed for English often fall short when applied to Bangla, highlighting the need for language-specific approaches. Previous efforts to address Bangla readability have largely focused on adapting existing English readability formulas (Islam & Islam, 2013; Rahman et al., 2014). These adaptations often rely on simple word and sentence length calculations, overlooking critical linguistic features specific to Bangla that influence comprehension. Moreover, these studies frequently treat readability as an inherent property of the text itself, neglecting the crucial role of the *reader* in the readability equation. An individual's educational background, prior knowledge, and linguistic proficiency significantly shape their ability to understand a given text. What is considered “readable” for a highly educated native speaker may pose significant challenges for someone with limited formal education or a different linguistic background. This paper addresses these limitations by examining the influence of both target reader background and intrinsic text features on perceived readability in Bangla. We hypothesize that the interplay between these factors is crucial in accurately assessing reading difficulty. To investigate this hypothesis, we present a novel, carefully constructed Bangla readability dataset, meticulously annotated by readers from two distinct background groups. This dataset, comprised of 135 Bangla documents, allows us to directly compare readability perceptions across different reader profiles. We systematically identify and analyze 20 text features categorized as “classic” (e.g., sentence length, word frequency) and “non-classic” (e.g., morphological complexity, use of conjunct verbs) – the latter being particularly relevant to the intricacies of the Bangla language. Through correlation analysis, we reveal varying influences of these features on perceived text hardness across the two reader groups. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive investigation into the interplay of reader background and text features in Bangla readability, thus contributing a foundational step towards developing more accurate and user-centric readability assessment tools for this widely spoken language. CCR, also known as entity linking or coreference, aims to identify all mentions referring to the same real-world entity across a collection of documents (Kilgour and Moffat, 2003; Nadeau and Sekine, 2007). Traditionally, CCR and NEL have been treated as largely independent problems, with separate algorithms and pipelines developed for each. Standard CCR systems rely on features such as string similarity, syntactic constraints, and contextual information to cluster mentions within and across documents (Ng and McCallum, 2001; Flanigan et al., 2014). NEL systems, conversely, leverage knowledge base information – entity popularity, textual descriptions, and relationships with other entities – to disambiguate mentions (Milne et al., 2008; Hoffart et al., 2011). response: Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm in deep learning, demonstrating substantial improvements across diverse natural language processing (NLP) tasks (Caruana, 1997; Collobert et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2016). The core idea behind MTL is that learning multiple related tasks simultaneously allows the model to leverage shared representations, leading to better generalization and performance compared to learning each task in isolation. A particularly effective approach within MTL involves neural networks, where shared layers are employed to extract common features, followed by task-specific layers for individual predictions (Yang & Yang, 2017; Pham et al., 2018). However, a significant challenge in neural network-based MTL lies in effectively managing the flow of information between tasks. While simply linking layers encourages knowledge sharing, it doesn't address the issue of *what* information should be shared. Naively sharing features can lead to negative transfer, where the presence of irrelevant or misleading features from one task degrades the performance of others (Ruder et al., 2017). This interference stems from the fact that different tasks often operate in distinct feature spaces, and forcing the model to share all features can contaminate these spaces with noise. Consequently, the model may struggle to discern the most relevant features for each task, hindering its ability to make accurate predictions. Existing work has attempted to alleviate this interference through various techniques. Some methods focus on learning task relationships to dynamically weight the importance of shared features (Zhao et al., 2016). Others employ regularization techniques to encourage task-specific representations (Chen et al., 2018). However, these approaches often require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not fully address the fundamental problem of feature selection – deciding *which* features to share and *when* to share them. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the learned leak parameters provide valuable insights into the relationships between tasks and the importance of different features. This work not only presents a practical method for improving multi-task learning performance but also contributes to a deeper understanding of how information should be shared in neural networks.

From assessing public opinion on social media to estimating disease incidence rates from clinical records, accurate prevalence estimation provides critical insights. This task, often referred to as class prevalence estimation, differs from traditional supervised classification where labeled data is readily available. Instead, it requires inferring the proportion of instances belonging to each class solely from the unlabeled collection itself. Early approaches to prevalence estimation largely relied on techniques like expectation-maximization (EM) algorithms applied to latent class models (e.g., Bishop, 2006). However, the performance of these methods is heavily dependent on strong assumptions about the underlying data distribution, which are often violated in real-world scenarios. More recently, a prevalent paradigm has been to aggregate predictions from multiple discriminative classifiers, and then calibrate or adjust these predictions to obtain point estimates of prevalence (e.g., Bart et al., 2012; Chen & Guestrin, 2016). While these methods have shown promising empirical results, a crucial limitation remains: they typically fail to adequately quantify the *uncertainty* associated with the estimated prevalence. In many scientific and practical applications, providing a point estimate alone is insufficient. Knowing the range of plausible prevalence values—expressed, for example, through confidence intervals—is essential for sound decision-making and statistically valid inference. Simply calibrating classifier outputs rarely yields well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, as it doesn’t account for the inherent limitations and potential inaccuracies of the underlying classifiers. Imperfect classifier accuracy should naturally translate into uncertainty about the overall prevalence estimate. In this work, we address this critical gap by developing an uncertainty-aware framework for prevalence estimation. Our approach is grounded in a generative probabilistic modeling perspective, where we explicitly model the likelihood of observing the unlabeled data given different prevalence distributions. While reading, people don’t simply absorb words in a linear fashion; they actively construct hierarchical representations of sentence structure (Frazier, 1987; Gibson, 2000). Understanding the cognitive mechanisms underlying this process is a central goal of psycholinguistic research, and a key component of this understanding lies in quantifying the incremental difficulty of parsing a sentence. This difficulty isn’t uniform; some sentence structures are easier to process than others, leading to variations in reading times and other behavioral measures. One approach to modeling these difficulties is through the development of *complexity metrics* – quantitative measures that attempt to predict processing load based on structural properties of the sentence. Specifically, *surprisal* – the negative log probability assigned to a word given its preceding context – has emerged as a strong predictor of reading times (Levy, 2008). The intuition behind surprisal is that lower probabilities indicate more unexpected words, and therefore, greater processing effort. Chart-based parsers, which maintain a complete representation of all possible parse trees, are frequently used to calculate these probabilities. Hierarchical Hidden Markov Models (HHMMs) offer an appealing alternative. HHMMs utilize a bounded model of working memory, pursuing multiple, parallel hypotheses in an incremental fashion – mirroring aspects of human cognition (Roark et al., 2001; Hale, 2001). response: Native Language Identification (NLI), the task of determining an author’s first language based on their writing in a second language (L2), has garnered increasing attention within the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community. This is driven by applications ranging from personalized language learning and automated essay scoring, to forensic linguistics and authorship attribution. Existing approaches frequently frame NLI as a classification problem, leveraging the characteristic errors and stylistic patterns exhibited by non-native speakers. Typically, these methods rely on relatively simple features, such as character n-grams (for small, fixed *n*), unigram frequencies of function words, and part-of-speech (PoS) tag sequences (Tetlow & Cook, 2015; Van Halteren, 2000). While effective to a degree, these features often fail to capture the more subtle and long-range dependencies that distinguish native and non-native writing. Recent research suggests that longer-range syntactic patterns can be particularly indicative of an author’s linguistic background. For example, approximations of syntactic complexity and the frequency of specific syntactic structures have demonstrated correlation with native language proficiency (Lu, 2010; McNamara & Hawkes, 2010). However, explicitly modeling such patterns with traditional methods often necessitates defining a fixed set of syntactic features, restricting the system's ability to discover potentially important, but unseen, constructions. To address this limitation, we explore the use of *adaptor grammars* (Pereira & Riley, 1997) as a mechanism for dynamically capturing collocations of arbitrary length, combining both lexical (words) and syntactic (PoS tags) information. Adaptor grammars offer a probabilistic framework for learning and recognizing variable-length sequences, providing a flexible alternative to fixed-n-gram models and pre-defined syntactic features. The core idea is to ‘adapt’ a grammar to the observed data, learning which sequences are statistically significant indicators of a given native language. In this work, we investigate two distinct approaches for integrating adaptor grammars into an NLI system. First, we explore the use of adaptor grammars to derive features—specifically, the probabilities of learned collocations—for a maximum entropy (maxent) classifier. By learning syntactic structures directly from the data, ISLMs offer a potentially more robust representation of linguistic patterns. response: Achieving a deep understanding of natural language requires moving beyond simply identifying the words in a sentence to understanding their meanings and relationships. Two crucial tasks in this endeavor are Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) and Semantic Role Labeling (SRL). Word Sense Disambiguation aims to identify the correct meaning of a word in context, resolving ambiguity arising from polysemy – the ability of a word to have multiple meanings. Semantic Role Labeling, on the other hand, focuses on identifying the semantic roles of constituents in a sentence with respect to a predicate (typically a verb), effectively answering “who did what to whom, when, and where.” Both tasks contribute significantly to a sentence-level semantic representation, which is vital for applications like machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. Traditionally, WSD and SRL have been addressed as separate, largely independent problems. Systems typically operate in a pipeline, where WSD is performed first, and its output is then used as input to the SRL system, or vice versa. While this pipeline approach has yielded considerable progress, it inherently overlooks the strong logical connections that exist between these two tasks. The correct sense of a word often influences the possible semantic roles it can fulfill, and conversely, the semantic role a constituent plays can provide clues about the intended sense of the words within that constituent. For example, knowing that a word is functioning as an Agent in a sentence strengthens the likelihood that it’s being used in a particular sense related to intentional action. Recent studies have begun to explore the benefits of integrating WSD and SRL. Initial investigations, often relying on pipeline architectures with feedback loops, have demonstrated that performing automatic all-word sense disambiguation can indeed improve semantic role labeling performance, and improvements in SRL can positively impact WSD accuracy (e.g., Surdeanu et al., 2007; O’Hara & Whittaker, 2011). These findings underscore the inherent synergy between the tasks, motivating the development of more tightly coupled modeling approaches. In this paper, we move beyond these pipeline-based approaches and propose a novel framework for jointly modeling WSD and SRL using Markov Logic – a powerful formalism that combines first-order logic with probabilistic graphical models. This allows us to explicitly represent and reason about the logical constraints that govern the relationship between word senses and semantic roles. By leveraging these constraints, our model aims to achieve higher performance in both tasks than traditional pipeline systems. We evaluate our joint model on the widely used OntoNotes 3.0 dataset, demonstrating that it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art pipeline approaches for both word sense disambiguation and semantic role labeling. Our findings underscore the benefits of a unified approach to semantic analysis, revealing that explicitly modeling the interplay between WSD and SRL offers a substantial improvement in overall performance. response: Information Retrieval (IR) has long been a central research area within Computer Science, aiming to provide users with relevant documents in response to their information needs, typically expressed as queries. Traditional IR models, such as the Vector Space Model (Salton & McGill, 1983), largely rely on lexical matching – identifying documents containing terms present in the query. However, this approach often falls short in capturing the semantic nuances of language, leading to issues of synonymy (different words with the same meaning) and polysemy (the same word with different meanings). For instance, a query containing the term “car” might benefit from retrieving documents discussing “automobile”, despite the lack of exact lexical overlap. To address these limitations, researchers have explored the incorporation of lexical semantic knowledge into IR systems for decades (Sparck Jones, 1972). Early approaches often relied on manually constructed thesauri, like WordNet (Fellbaum, 1998), which define relationships between words such as synonymy, hypernymy (is-a relationship), and hyponymy (has-a relationship). These resources have proven valuable in various IR tasks, including query expansion and relevance ranking. However, the creation and maintenance of such manually curated lexicons are often costly and time-consuming, and their coverage can be limited, especially for emerging terminology or specialized domains. Recently, a new wave of collaborative knowledge bases has emerged, offering a potentially richer and more dynamic source of lexical semantic information. Wikipedia, a freely editable online encyclopedia, and Wiktionary, its sister project focused on lexical definitions, represent particularly promising resources. These platforms are built and maintained by a large community of contributors, resulting in extensive coverage and continuous updates. Unlike traditional thesauri, their knowledge is inherently contextualized within the encyclopedic entries and definitions, potentially offering a more nuanced understanding of word meanings. Despite their potential, the optimal way to leverage these collaborative knowledge bases for IR remains an open question. Simply incorporating all available semantic relations might introduce noise or prioritize less relevant connections. A crucial step is to understand *which* types of lexical semantic relations between query and document terms are most indicative of relevance. This paper aims to address this gap by analyzing the semantic relationships that exist between query terms and document terms, and evaluating how different measures of semantic relatedness can capture these relationships. response: Coreference resolution, the task of identifying mentions in text that refer to the same entity, is a fundamental problem in natural language processing with applications ranging from information extraction and question answering to machine translation and summarization. Despite significant progress in recent years (Soon et al., 2001;Ng and Cardie, 2002;Manning and Klein, 2003), coreference resolution remains a challenging task. A key difficulty lies in distinguishing between *anaphoric* mentions – those that refer back to previously introduced entities – and *non-anaphoric* mentions, such as those introduced without prior reference or those referring to general concepts (e.g., “the president” as a role, not a specific individual). Recent research suggests that explicitly identifying and filtering out these non-anaphoric mentions *prior* to the coreference linking stage can dramatically improve the performance of a coreference system (Durme et al., 2006;Denis and Maxwell, 2006). Intuitively, preventing a coreference system from attempting to link non-anaphoric mentions reduces spurious links and allows it to focus on genuine coreference relations. However, accurately determining anaphoricity is itself a non-trivial problem. Graph cuts provide a principled and globally optimal framework for segmenting data based on pairwise costs (Boykov and Jolly, 2001). We formulate the anaphoricity determination problem as a graph cut, where nodes represent mentions and edges represent the cost of labeling two mentions as either both anaphoric or one anaphoric and one non-anaphoric. Within this flexibility lies a curious phenomenon: the consistent and pervasive use of vulgar language, despite its often-explicit social prohibition. This prevalence raises a fundamental question: why do people swear? The answer, as linguistic and psychological research suggests, is rarely simple. Understanding these nuanced functions is crucial not only for theoretical linguistics and social psychology, but also for a growing number of practical applications in Natural Language Processing (NLP). The versatility of vulgarity presents a significant challenge for computational systems. Traditional sentiment analysis, for instance, often flags swear words as inherently negative, overlooking instances where they are used playfully, empathetically, or ironically. Similarly, toxicity detection models may incorrectly classify seemingly innocuous sentences containing vulgar terms as hostile. This misinterpretation can lead to biased outcomes in applications like content moderation, social media monitoring, and even therapeutic chatbots. Current NLP systems struggle to discern the *intention* behind the use of vulgar language, treating it primarily as a surface-level marker of negativity, and failing to capture the rich pragmatic context that shapes its meaning. Despite the obvious importance of understanding this phenomenon, quantitative research leveraging computational techniques is surprisingly limited. It is a crucial component in many natural language processing (NLP) applications, including knowledge base construction, question answering, and information retrieval. Traditionally, RE relies on manually annotated datasets, which are expensive and time-consuming to create. Distantly supervised relation extraction (DS-RE) offers a promising alternative by leveraging existing knowledge bases (KBs) to automatically generate training data. While DS-RE avoids manual annotation, it inevitably introduces noise due to the incorrect labeling of instances—a key challenge hindering its performance. Existing DS-RE approaches often employ multi-instance learning (MIL) frameworks where each sentence containing an entity pair is treated as a bag of instances (words) and at least one instance in the bag is assumed to be positive if the sentence is labeled as expressing a relation between the entities. Attention mechanisms have become increasingly popular within these frameworks to mitigate the impact of noisy instances. By selectively focusing on the most relevant parts of a sentence, attention can help identify valid instances and filter out noise. However, many current attention models operate on 1-dimensional vectors, representing the entire sentence or aspects of it as a single, flattened representation. This approach can struggle to fully capture the complex, multi-faceted contexts necessary for effectively distinguishing between valid and noisy instances. response: Cross-lingual transfer, the ability to leverage resources from one language to improve performance in another, is a central challenge in natural language processing. One promising approach to this challenge involves learning joint embeddings of text from different languages, such that semantically similar phrases are mapped to nearby points in a shared vector space (Bengio et al., 2014; Mikolov et al., 2013; Xing et al., 2015). Traditionally, such embeddings are learned from parallel corpora – aligned text in multiple languages. However, the availability of large-scale parallel data is limited for most language pairs, hindering the widespread application of these techniques. Recent work has explored utilizing monolingual data and leveraging intermediate resources to bridge the gap between languages. Images provide a particularly compelling intermediate representation, as they offer a modality that is largely independent of language and readily available in large quantities, paired with descriptive text in multiple languages (Feng et al., 2015; Lazaridou et al., 2014). Bilingual image tags, for instance, explicitly link concepts across languages through a shared visual grounding. Building on this insight, we propose a novel approach to learning bilingual text embeddings by conditioning their induction on shared visual information. At the heart of our approach lies Partial Canonical Correlation Analysis (PCCA) (Hotelling, 1936). PCCA is a statistical technique that finds linear projections of two variables such that their correlation is maximized, given a third shared variable. In our context, the two variables are the text embeddings for the two languages, and the shared variable is the visual representation. While powerful, standard PCCA is limited by its linearity, potentially failing to capture the complex non-linear relationships present in high-dimensional text and image data. To address this, we introduce Deep PCCA (DPCCA), a non-linear extension of PCCA leveraging the expressive power of deep neural networks. Crucially, optimizing DPCCA presents a significant challenge. The original PCCA has a closed-form solution, but DPCCA requires an iterative optimization procedure. We develop a novel stochastic iterative algorithm specifically tailored for DPCCA, ensuring efficient and stable convergence. This algorithm alternates between learning the text embeddings, learning the visual embedding, and performing a PCCA-like alignment step in the learned feature space. We evaluate our models on multilingual word similarity and cross-lingual image description retrieval tasks. Demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach, DPCCA consistently outperforms a wide range of competing methods, including those based on distributional similarity and canonical correlation analysis. These relationships, often signaled by discourse connectives (e.g., “but,” “because,” “therefore”), contribute significantly to coherence and meaning. While substantial progress has been made in automatically analyzing English discourse, particularly with resources like the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) (Prasad et al., 2008), discourse analysis for languages like Chinese presents unique challenges. Chinese discourse lacks explicit markers – such as conjunctions – as commonly found in English, relying heavily on implicit cues and word order. This makes identifying discourse relations more difficult and necessitates specialized annotation schemes and resources. Existing work on Chinese discourse analysis has explored various approaches. Some studies have focused on identifying discourse connectives (Zheng and Zhou, 2010), while others have attempted to adapt existing English-based frameworks (Li et al., 2013). However, directly applying these frameworks often fails to capture the nuances of Chinese discourse, particularly the importance of dependency relations and the subtle interplay between connectives and rhetorical structure. For example, rhetorical relations, as defined by Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) (Mann and Thompson, 1988), provide a hierarchical representation of a text’s communicative intentions. Encoding this hierarchical structure effectively is crucial for discourse understanding. The CDT integrates the benefits of dependency parsing with the explicit representation of discourse connectives, inspired by both the PDTB and RST. Current evaluation methodologies largely fall into two categories: extrinsic and intrinsic. Extrinsic evaluation assesses the quality of embeddings by their performance on downstream tasks, such as text classification or machine translation. While valuable, extrinsic evaluation is often time-consuming and task-dependent, making it difficult to directly compare different embedding models. Intrinsic evaluation, on the other hand, aims to assess the quality of embeddings by examining their internal structure, without relying on external tasks. Existing intrinsic evaluations typically focus on measuring the similarity between words – for example, testing whether synonyms have similar vectors, or whether analogies hold (e.g., “king – man + woman ≈ queen”). These approaches largely treat word vectors as points in a high-dimensional space, focusing on overall vector similarity. However, this “point-based” view overlooks the crucial notion that linguistic relationships are often expressed through *subspaces* within the vector space. For example, the difference between “king” and “man” might lie primarily within a subspace representing gender, while the difference between “king” and “queen” might capture a different linguistic dimension such as royalty. response: The web has become an invaluable resource for a vast range of information, but extracting structured data from it remains a significant challenge. A key component of this extraction process is entity mention mining – the task of identifying textual spans that refer to specific real-world entities. While sophisticated Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, particularly those leveraging deep learning, have made substantial progress on this front, they often struggle with the inherent noise and variability present in web-sourced data. Unlike curated datasets, web documents exhibit a diverse range of writing styles, formatting inconsistencies, and often contain errors introduced during automated generation or data entry. This poses a particular challenge for tasks involving entity types that inherently conform to structured patterns – dates, times, email addresses, product codes, and course numbers, to name a few. Traditionally, Regular Expressions (REs) have been a go-to approach for identifying these pattern-based entities. Their expressive power allows for the precise definition of expected formats. However, the real world is rarely so neat. Exhaustively defining REs to cover all possible variations of even seemingly simple entity types like dates – consider the myriad of formats like “MM/DD/YYYY”, “DD-Mon-YY”, or even “January 1st, 2024” – is a daunting, often impossible task. Any attempt to create a single, comprehensive RE inevitably leads to trade-offs between precision and recall; a highly precise RE may miss legitimate instances, while a broad RE may incorrectly identify non-entity spans. Despite these limitations, abandoning REs altogether seems ill-advised. They represent a valuable source of prior knowledge about the expected form of entities and provide a strong initial signal that can be leveraged by more advanced techniques. Rather than viewing REs and deep learning as mutually exclusive approaches, we propose a novel framework that integrates the strengths of both. Our work is motivated by the observation that while REs alone may not achieve perfect accuracy, they can efficiently generate weak labels on a large scale, providing a strong foundation for training a neural network model. This paper presents a framework that systematically combines RE-driven weak supervision, deep learning, and a modest amount of human expertise. We begin by either curating or collecting existing REs for a target entity type. These REs are then applied to a large corpus of web documents to automatically generate initial entity mention labels. A neural network is trained to predict these RE-generated labels, effectively learning to recognize the patterns encoded in the REs and generalize to similar instances. Critically, we recognize that the initial labels are inherently noisy. To address this, we incorporate a human-in-the-loop component, where a human expert labels a small, representative subset of the data. This curated data is then used to fine-tune the neural network, effectively correcting the errors introduced by the initial weak supervision. Our experimental evaluation on several entity identification tasks demonstrates the effectiveness of this integrated approach. We show that our framework achieves impressive accuracy, outperforming baseline methods, while significantly reducing the human labeling effort required to achieve comparable results. This approach represents a practical and scalable solution for entity mention mining from the noisy and diverse landscape of the web.

A core component of phrase-based SMT systems is the decoding process, which seeks the most probable target language sequence given a source language sentence according to a statistical model. Traditionally, this decoding is performed in a left-to-right (LTR) fashion, mirroring the typical linear order of words in many languages. However, the assumption of a universally optimal decoding direction is not necessarily warranted. Languages exhibit significant structural diversity, and word order is not uniform across all languages. Some languages are predominantly head-initial (like English), while others are head-final (like Japanese or Turkish). These differences in linguistic typology suggest that a decoding strategy optimized for one language might be suboptimal for another. Further, the interaction between source and target language structure could be critical, and a single decoding direction might struggle to capture this interplay effectively. This paper challenges the conventional wisdom of left-to-right decoding in phrase-based SMT. We hypothesize that the optimal decoding direction is language-pair specific and that a more robust approach involves integrating information from both decoding directions. To this end, we systematically investigate the performance of a right-to-left (RTL) decoder alongside the standard LTR decoder. Crucially, we conduct a large-scale evaluation across a diverse set of 272 language pairs – significantly expanding upon prior limited investigations of decoding directionality. Our findings reveal a surprising result: for the vast majority of the language pairs studied, decoding from right-to-left *outperforms* decoding from left-to-right. This initially counterintuitive observation highlights the crucial role of target language structure in the translation process. Furthermore, we introduce and evaluate a bidirectional decoding strategy that combines the outputs of both LTR and RTL decoders. Specifically, bidirectional decoding yielded a BLEU score improvement over LTR decoding in 99% of our experimental runs, confirming its effectiveness and generality. Our work provides strong evidence that decoding direction is not merely an implementation detail, but a substantive factor influencing translation quality. It also proposes a simple, yet effective, method for improving SMT performance by intelligently integrating information from both decoding directions.

response: Opinion mining, the computational task of identifying and extracting subjective information from text, has matured considerably in recent years. Early work focused primarily on sentiment polarity classification – determining whether a text expresses a positive or negative opinion (Turney, 2002; Pang et al., 2002). However, a nuanced understanding of opinions requires more than simply identifying polarity. Fine-grained opinion mining aims to identify *what* opinions are expressed, *who* holds them, and *towards what* entities or aspects they are directed (Liu, 2012). This involves identifying opinion holders, opinion targets, and the specific opinions expressed about those targets – often referred to as opinion frames. For instance, understanding that “The battery life is terrible” expresses a negative opinion (“terrible”) held by an unstated user, towards the “battery life” of a product, represents a significant step beyond simple polarity detection. The majority of research in opinion mining has focused on resource-rich languages, particularly English, due to the availability of large labeled datasets and sophisticated NLP tools. However, the global nature of online content necessitates opinion mining capabilities across multiple languages. Building supervised opinion mining systems for each language individually is a costly and time-consuming process, requiring substantial human annotation efforts. Cross-lingual opinion mining (CLOM) offers a solution by leveraging resources from one or more source languages to perform opinion mining in a target language with limited or no labeled data. Several approaches to CLOM have been proposed. These include machine translation-based approaches, which translate the target language text into a source language, perform opinion mining on the translated text, and then potentially translate the results back to the target language (Lin et al., 2009). Another approach leverages cross-lingual word embeddings to transfer knowledge from a source language to a target language (Glorot et al., 2011). However, these methods often suffer from error propagation due to translation inaccuracies or limitations in the quality of cross-lingual embeddings. response: Entity linking (EL), also known as entity disambiguation, is the task of associating mentions of entities in unstructured text with their corresponding entries in a knowledge base (KB) such as Wikipedia or Freebase. This is a crucial step in many information extraction (IE) pipelines, effectively bridging the gap between natural language text and structured knowledge. A successful entity linking system allows users to seamlessly access rich encyclopedic information, improving the user experience in applications like search engines, question answering systems, and document summarization. For example, given the mention “Apple” in a news article, an EL system should correctly identify whether it refers to the technology company or the fruit. Early approaches to entity linking relied heavily on rule-based methods and dictionary lookups (Gaizauskas et al., 2008; Milne and Milne, 2008). These approaches often struggle with ambiguity and require extensive manual engineering. More recently, machine learning techniques have become dominant. A common paradigm is to formulate entity linking as a classification problem (Ratinov et al., 2009; Hoffart et al., 2011). In this framework, each candidate entity is assigned a class label (relevant or irrelevant) based on a set of features extracted from the mention, the context, and the candidate entity itself. However, we argue that framing entity linking as a classification problem is suboptimal. In many real-world scenarios, there are multiple plausible candidates for a given mention. The goal isn't simply to determine whether an entity is relevant, but rather to *rank* the candidates by their likelihood of being the correct referent. This allows a system to return a list of potential entities, ordered by confidence, providing the user with more comprehensive and nuanced information. Furthermore, considering the relationships between candidate entities – leveraging the structure of the knowledge base itself – is often critical for accurate disambiguation. For instance, if several candidates are related to “Steve Jobs”, the probability of a candidate being “Apple Inc.” is significantly higher. In this paper, we propose a learning-to-rank (LTR) algorithm specifically designed for entity linking. Our approach moves beyond the binary classification framework and directly optimizes for ranking accuracy. We incorporate features that explicitly model the relationships between candidate entities within the KB, enabling the system to exploit the interconnectedness of knowledge. We evaluate our approach on the TAC 2009 dataset, a widely used benchmark for entity linking. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, achieving an 18.5% improvement in accuracy over classification-based models for entities with corresponding KB entries. Moreover, the overall system performance surpasses that of existing state-of-the-art entity linking systems, highlighting the benefits of our learning-to-rank framework and relationship-aware feature engineering. response: Automated negotiation is a challenging task at the intersection of artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and game theory. It requires agents to not only reason about their opponent’s preferences and beliefs, but also to effectively communicate their own, leveraging the nuances of natural language to reach mutually beneficial agreements. Recent years have witnessed significant progress in this field, spurred by the availability of increasingly complex negotiation environments and the development of powerful neural models (Lewis et al., 2017; Futeral & Holmes, 2018; Zhang et al., 2019). However, a key limitation of existing approaches, particularly those relying on end-to-end neural networks, lies in the difficulty of controlling the *strategy* employed during negotiation. These models learn to map directly from dialogue history to utterances, making it challenging to intervene and explicitly guide the negotiation process towards specific goals or behaviors. While reinforcement learning (RL) offers a potential path to learning optimal negotiation strategies, it frequently suffers from issues such as reward sparsity and the tendency to converge to degenerate solutions, often involving repetitive or uninformative dialogue (Li et al., 2016). For instance, an RL agent might discover that repeatedly proposing the same offer, albeit suboptimal, is sufficient to secure a reward in a specific training environment, neglecting the potential for more sophisticated negotiation tactics. This underscores the need for more structured and interpretable approaches to negotiation dialogue. In this paper, we argue for a modular approach to negotiation dialogue that explicitly *decouples* strategy and generation. Our core idea is to represent the negotiation strategy at a high level, using a set of coarse-grained dialogue acts (e.g., propose(price=50), accept(), reject()), and then independently generate natural language utterances that realize these acts. This separation allows for greater flexibility in controlling the strategic behavior of the agent, enabling us to leverage a variety of techniques – supervised learning, reinforcement learning, or even domain-specific knowledge – to determine the optimal sequence of dialogue acts without encountering the degeneracy issues that plague end-to-end RL approaches. We demonstrate that this decoupling promotes control, robustness, and the ability to generate compelling and effective negotiation dialogue. As robots move from performing simple, pre-programmed tasks to assisting humans in more complex, collaborative endeavors, the quality of the interaction becomes paramount. A crucial aspect of successful HRI is a natural and efficient dialogue system, enabling seamless communication between human and robot. While many HRI systems focus on the robot’s capabilities – its sensing, planning, and acting – comparatively less attention has been paid to the usability of the *interface* through which humans control and collaborate with these systems, specifically through dialogue. Evaluating the usability of a dialogue system is a complex undertaking. Traditionally, usability assessment has relied on a combination of subjective measures, such as user satisfaction questionnaires, and objective measures, derived from system logs and interaction data. Subjective measures capture the user’s overall perception of the system, their feelings of ease of use, and their overall satisfaction. However, these measures can be influenced by a variety of factors unrelated to the system itself, such as the user’s prior experience or mood. Objective measures, on the other hand, provide quantifiable data about the interaction itself – dialogue length, error rates, task completion time – offering a potentially more grounded assessment of usability. Despite the availability of both types of measures, it remains unclear which aspects of a human-robot dialogue are most critical to user satisfaction. Identifying these critical factors is vital for prioritizing design efforts and ensuring that future HRI systems are truly user-centric. This paper addresses this question by presenting a study of a human-robot dialogue system designed to facilitate a collaborative task: building wooden construction toys. Among the various components within an SMT system, phrase-based translation (Koehn et al., 2003; Marcu et al., 2006) has proven particularly effective, breaking down sentences into smaller, manageable segments – phrases – and translating them individually before reordering them to produce fluent target language output. A crucial component within phrase-based SMT is the reordering model, responsible for determining the optimal order of target phrases given the source phrases. Accurate reordering is particularly critical for language pairs with substantial differences in word order, such as Chinese and English. Early reordering models relied on simple rules and heuristics (Brown et al., 1993). Later, lexicalized reordering models emerged as a significant improvement (Tillmann et al., 2004; Galley et al., 2006). These models incorporate lexical information, learning reordering probabilities conditioned on the source and target words within a phrase pair. While effective, lexicalized reordering models suffer from several limitations. First, they are inherently context-insensitive, treating each phrase pair in isolation and failing to leverage information from surrounding phrase pairs. This can lead to suboptimal reordering decisions, especially in longer sentences where global context is important. Second, reordering ambiguity - when multiple reordering possibilities exist - is not adequately addressed, potentially leading to incorrect phrase arrangement. Finally, and perhaps most significantly, lexicalized models suffer from data sparsity. As the vocabulary size grows, the number of possible lexical combinations increases exponentially, making it difficult to estimate reliable reordering probabilities for all phrase pairs, particularly for rare or unseen lexical items. To address these limitations, we propose a novel neural reordering model. Our model explicitly incorporates contextual information by conditioning reordering probabilities not only on the current phrase pair, but also on the words of *previous* phrase pairs. This allows the model to learn dependencies between adjacent phrases, improving context sensitivity and reducing reordering ambiguity. Instead of building a separate reordering model for each phrase pair, we train a single neural network to classify all phrase pairs. We demonstrate that by incorporating contextual information and adopting a unified classifier, we can learn a more robust and accurate reordering model for phrase-based machine translation. response: Commonsense reasoning is a hallmark of human intelligence, allowing us to navigate the world with an understanding of unstated assumptions and typical situations. Replicating this ability in machines remains a significant challenge in Artificial Intelligence. A key component of commonsense is *knowledge* – not specialized expertise, but rather the vast network of everyday facts and relationships most humans acquire during childhood. While large-scale knowledge bases (KBs) like WordNet (Miller, 1995) and Cyc (Lenat, 1995) have attempted to capture this information, their construction has proven to be laborious, expensive, and often incomplete. More recently, automatically constructed KBs have emerged as a promising alternative. One such resource is ConceptNet (Speer and Havasi, 2012), a semantic network built from the Open Mind Common Sense project and other sources. ConceptNet focuses on representing commonsense knowledge through assertions of the form (subject, relation, object), for example, (“dog”, “isA”, “mammal”) or (“eat”, “usedFor”, “nutrition”). Unlike traditional KBs, ConceptNet doesn’t restrict its entities to a predefined set; it allows for arbitrary phrases, making it more flexible yet also presenting new challenges. However, ConceptNet, like any automatically constructed KB, contains noise and incompleteness. Many valid commonsense assertions are missing, and spurious or inaccurate relationships inevitably exist. In this work, we address the problem of enriching ConceptNet by framing it as a *knowledge base completion (KBC)* task. KBC traditionally focuses on predicting missing relations between entities already present in a KB (Bordes et al., 2013; Socher et al., 2013). However, adapting standard KBC techniques to ConceptNet is non-trivial due to its open entity space. Most existing KBC models rely on embedding entities within a fixed vocabulary. Finally, Section 5 presents a qualitative analysis and discusses the implications of our findings.

response: The proliferation of social media platforms has created a vast and dynamic corpus of user-generated text, reflecting a diverse range of linguistic variation. While this presents exciting opportunities for Natural Language Processing (NLP) research, it also poses significant challenges. Traditional NLP tools are often developed and evaluated on standardized, formal language, and frequently exhibit diminished performance when applied to the more informal and dialectal language prevalent online (Eisenstein, 2013; Blodgett & Ruppenhofer, 2014). This performance gap is particularly pronounced for under-represented dialects, hindering equitable access to NLP technologies and exacerbating existing social inequalities. A particularly salient example of this challenge is the presence of African-American English (AAE) on social media. AAE is a systematic and rule-governed dialect of English with a rich history and distinct linguistic features (Rickford & Rickford, 2000; Wolfram & Schilling-Estes, 2006). Its use in online communication is widespread, particularly on platforms like Twitter, where users have greater freedom to express themselves in their vernacular. However, existing NLP tools often fail to accurately process AAE, leading to errors in tasks such as sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and machine translation. This is due, in part, to a lack of sufficient training data reflecting AAE characteristics and a bias towards mainstream English in the development of many NLP algorithms. This work addresses this gap by presenting a detailed case study of AAE on Twitter. Our investigation focuses on automatically identifying AAE-like language usage based on demographic information associated with geo-located tweets, specifically leveraging user-reported demographics. We hypothesize that analyzing the language patterns correlated with these demographic indicators can provide a scalable approach to identifying and studying AAE in online contexts. Critically, we do not assume automatic identification *is* accurate AAE usage; instead, we evaluate whether the identified language aligns with established linguistic features of AAE. We develop a distantly supervised model to achieve this identification, and validate its output by demonstrating a correspondence with well-documented AAE linguistic phenomena, such as copula deletion and habitual *be* (Green, 2002). To mitigate this issue, we propose and evaluate an ensemble classifier for language identification specifically designed to improve performance on AAE-like text, thereby leveling the playing field. Finally, recognizing the need for dedicated resources, we release a new corpus of tweets containing AAE-like language, alongside the software tools used in our analysis to facilitate further research in this rapidly evolving area. Our contributions aim to provide a foundation for developing more inclusive and equitable NLP technologies capable of effectively processing the diverse linguistic landscape of social media.

response: Dependency parsing is a fundamental task in natural language processing, aiming to uncover the grammatical structure of a sentence by establishing relationships between words. Accurate dependency parses are crucial components for various downstream applications, including machine translation, information extraction, and question answering. Traditional approaches to dependency parsing often rely on feature-rich models, specifically those leveraging high-order features that capture complex interactions between words and their contextual information (McDonald & Nivre, 2007; Eisner, 2003; Kübler et al., 2007). However, incorporating such features introduces significant computational challenges, as the inference problem becomes non-convex and, in many cases, NP-hard (McDonald et al., 2005). Consequently, a substantial body of research has been dedicated to developing sophisticated optimization algorithms capable of tackling these complex decoding problems. Dual decomposition (Rush et al., 2010; Martins et al., 2011) and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling (Johnson, 2007; Goldberg & Nivre, 2012) have emerged as popular choices, offering effective, albeit computationally expensive, solutions. These methods typically involve iterative refinement processes, often requiring substantial training time and resources. In contrast to this trend of increasingly complex optimization strategies, we propose a surprisingly simple yet effective alternative: a randomized greedy inference algorithm. Our work challenges the prevailing assumption that optimal parsing necessitates elaborate decoding procedures. We hypothesize and demonstrate that, when properly randomized, a greedy approach can achieve near-optimal parsing performance, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. This paper makes several key contributions. First, we provide a theoretical analysis of the greedy method in the context of first-order dependency parsing. We analytically quantify the number of local optima the algorithm potentially faces, offering insights into its inherent limitations and potential for improvement. response: Statistical machine translation (SMT) has, for many years, been the dominant paradigm in automated translation. Early SMT systems relied heavily on word-based models (Brown et al., 1993), which, while successful, suffered from an inability to capture long-range dependencies or phrasal coherence. Phrase-based SMT (Koehn et al., 2003) addressed this limitation by directly modeling translational equivalence at the phrase level, leading to substantial improvements in translation quality. However, phrase-based models still require substantial engineering effort, including careful tuning of phrase extraction heuristics and distortion limits. More recently, syntax-based machine translation (Yamada & Knight, 2001; Chiang, 2005) has emerged as a promising alternative. These approaches aim to learn translation rules directly from syntactic parse trees of parallel corpora, offering the potential for more robust and generalizable translation models. A critical component of syntax-based MT is the induction of a synchronous grammar (SG), which formally defines the correspondences between the syntactic structures of source and target languages. This SG can then be used to generate translations by finding the most probable syntactic derivation. Despite the considerable potential of SG induction, several challenges remain. Existing approaches often rely on heuristics or constraints derived from word alignment models (e.g., Och & Ney, 2003). While these constraints can improve performance, they also introduce biases and limit the model’s ability to discover novel and potentially more accurate translation patterns. Furthermore, inference in SG models is computationally expensive. Traditional approaches often require enumerating over vast derivation forests, making them intractable for large-scale corpora. Attempts to mitigate this complexity typically involve approximations or simplifying assumptions that can degrade translation quality. In this paper, we present a novel approach to phrasal synchronous grammar induction that directly addresses these limitations. Unlike previous methods, we eschew external constraints from word alignment models and instead aim to learn the SG directly from parallel sentence-aligned corpora. We employ a hierarchical Bayesian prior that encourages the discovery of compact grammars with small translation units, promoting generalization and preventing overfitting. The core of our approach is a novel Gibbs sampler designed for efficient inference over synchronous derivations. Crucially, this sampler avoids the intractability issues associated with derivation forests by operating directly on individual derivations, making each sampling iteration significantly more efficient. This efficiency allows us to apply our model to larger translation corpora than previously possible, bringing us closer to realizing the full potential of synchronous grammar induction in statistical machine translation. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (1) a phrasal synchronous grammar model without reliance on word alignment heuristics; (2) a hierarchical Bayesian prior for compact grammar induction; and (3) a novel, computationally efficient Gibbs sampler for inference over synchronous derivations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on standard parallel corpora, showing competitive performance compared to existing methods. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work in synchronous grammar induction and statistical machine translation. Section 3 details our phrasal synchronous grammar model and Bayesian prior. Section 4 presents the Gibbs sampler inference procedure. Section 5 describes our experimental setup and results. Finally, Section 6 concludes with a discussion of future work.

Traditionally, language models operate at the word level, predicting the probability of a sequence of words. However, this approach often overlooks the rich structural information present within language, hindering its ability to capture long-range dependencies and subtle semantic nuances. Incorporating syntactic information into language models has long been recognized as a promising avenue for improvement (Chelba & Jelinek, 1998; Niesler & Ney, 2003), but doing so effectively presents significant challenges, particularly as the granularity of syntactic information increases. While coarse-grained Part-of-Speech (POS) tags have been successfully integrated into LMs (Mohan & Peng, 2002), they offer a relatively limited view of sentence structure. More detailed syntactic representations, such as those provided by full parse trees, are computationally expensive to process and often require sophisticated parsing pipelines that may not generalize well across languages. Supertagging, represented, for example, by the SuperARV tags (van Zaanen & Perlas, 2003), strikes a balance by offering a richer structural representation than POS tags while remaining computationally tractable. However, even Supertags can become unwieldy when dealing with very large tagsets and substantial corpora. Further, the creation of robust Supertaggers necessarily requires linguistic expertise and can be a bottleneck for adapting models to new languages. This paper introduces a scalable joint language model designed to leverage the benefits of fine-grain syntactic tags without succumbing to the scalability issues inherent in more complex approaches. We argue for the use of a carefully designed tagset – one that avoids the need for deep linguistic analysis while still providing meaningful structural information beyond the limitations of POS tags. Crucially, we propose tagsets that can be automatically derived from readily available, albeit imperfect, parse trees. This facilitates rapid prototyping and deployment of the model in new languages, lessening the reliance on costly and time-consuming manual annotation. Our approach addresses the challenges of training and deploying a joint LM with a large tagset by employing efficient data structures and prediction algorithms. We detail our solutions for handling the increased vocabulary size and computational complexity that arise with more granular syntactic representations. We present two novel fine-grain tagsets, built upon existing POS tags and augmented with information derived from constituency parse trees. These sets aim to provide a sweet spot between structural expressiveness and computational feasibility. We evaluate our model on a speech recognition task, comparing its performance with models that utilize POS tags, SuperARV tags, and a baseline word-level LM. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating fine-grain syntactic tags into the language model, highlighting the potential for significant improvements in downstream applications. Finally, we discuss future research directions, focusing on the integration of semantic information and the development of adaptive tagsets tailored to specific domains and languages.

response: The burgeoning field of sentiment analysis has witnessed significant advancements in recent years, propelled by the explosion of user-generated content online, particularly in the form of product reviews. These reviews offer a wealth of information about consumer opinions, preferences, and experiences, making sentiment analysis a vital tool for businesses seeking to understand their customers and improve their products. However, effectively extracting and interpreting sentiment from product reviews presents a series of challenges. Existing approaches, while often achieving reasonable accuracy, frequently fall short in leveraging the inherent structure within product domains and the nuanced ways sentiment is expressed regarding specific product attributes. A key limitation of many current sentiment analysis systems lies in their failure to fully utilize the hierarchical relationships between product attributes. For instance, when analyzing reviews of a laptop, a user might comment on the “screen,” which is a sub-attribute of the broader “display” attribute, itself falling under the overarching “hardware” category. Ignoring these hierarchical relationships can lead to an incomplete or inaccurate understanding of the review's overall sentiment. Current approaches often treat product attributes as independent entities, neglecting the contextual information provided by their relationships. Furthermore, existing methods often struggle with reviews that discuss multiple product attributes simultaneously, especially when those attributes are associated with complex or conflicting sentiments. A review stating, “The battery life is excellent, but the screen resolution is disappointing” expresses both positive and negative sentiment, relating to distinct attributes. Accurately dissecting such sentences and attributing the correct sentiment to each attribute requires a sophisticated understanding of the review's structure and the semantic relationships between different parts of the text. Simple bag-of-words or keyword-based approaches often fail to capture these nuances. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel Hierarchical Learning with Sentiment Ontology Tree (HL-SOT) approach for sentiment analysis in product reviews. Our method leverages a pre-defined Sentiment Ontology Tree (SOT) to encode the hierarchical relationships between product attributes and their associated sentiment polarities. This ontology serves as a structured knowledge base, guiding the learning process and enabling more accurate sentiment classification. The "Hierarchical Learning" component extends this to learn sentiment at various levels of granularity within the SOT, assigning sentiment not just to individual attributes, but also to broader categories and sub-categories. This paper details the HL-SOT framework, including the construction of the SOT, the hierarchical learning process, and the specific algorithms used for sentiment labeling. We evaluate the performance of our approach on a human-labeled dataset of product reviews, demonstrating its superior accuracy and effectiveness compared to existing methods. Moreover, while the primary focus of this work is on sentiment analysis for a single product category, we highlight the inherent scalability of HL-SOT and its potential for generalization to diverse product domains and mixed review sets. response: Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) is a challenging natural language processing task with significant practical applications, ranging from assisting language learners to improving the quality of written communication for native speakers. The goal of GEC is to automatically identify and correct grammatical errors in a given text, producing a fluent and grammatically correct revision. Over the past decade, two distinct approaches have emerged as particularly promising: machine learning classification and machine translation (MT). Both have achieved considerable success, driving substantial improvements in GEC performance, yet each possesses inherent strengths and weaknesses. The machine translation approach frames GEC as a translation problem, transforming incorrect sentences into correct ones, effectively treating grammatical errors as “noise” in the input language (Zellers et al., 2019). Trained on parallel corpora of incorrect and corrected sentences, MT models learn to map erroneous input to error-free output without explicitly relying on linguistic rules or feature engineering. This data-driven approach enables the system to capture complex grammatical patterns and stylistic preferences, proving adept at correcting intricate errors that may stump rule-based or feature-engineered systems. However, MT models inherently require large amounts of parallel data, a resource that is often limited and expensive to obtain. Furthermore, controlling the behavior of these models and incorporating specific linguistic knowledge can be difficult. In contrast, the classification approach tackles GEC by learning to identify and correct specific error types. This typically involves classifying spans of text as either correct or erroneous and then applying appropriate corrections based on pre-defined rules or learned patterns (Lee & Srikanta, 2011). Classification methods offer several advantages, including the ability to generalize better beyond the training data, the potential to leverage diverse knowledge sources (e.g., dictionaries, linguistic rules), and the flexibility to tailor correction strategies for individual error types. Moreover, classification-based systems can be trained without relying on parallel corpora, utilizing techniques like noisy channel modeling or distant supervision to generate training data automatically. However, they often struggle with complex errors requiring understanding of long-range dependencies or nuanced contextual information. Building on this insight, we propose a novel algorithmic approach that strategically combines MT and classification techniques to leverage their respective advantages. Our experiments demonstrate that this hybrid approach achieves substantial improvements over existing state-of-the-art GEC systems, achieving a relative improvement of over 20% and a 7.4 F-score point gain. This work underscores the value of integrating diverse machine learning paradigms to address complex NLP challenges like Grammatical Error Correction. response: Personalized search has become increasingly important as the volume of information available online continues to grow exponentially. Traditional information retrieval (IR) systems often treat all users equally, returning the same ranked list of results for a given query, irrespective of individual preferences. However, users have diverse information needs, and providing personalized search results can significantly improve user satisfaction and search efficiency (Agrawal et al., 2009;Radlinski & Joachims, 2005). A key component of personalized search is the creation of accurate and informative user profiles that represent a user’s interests and preferences. Existing approaches to user profile construction primarily rely on analyzing a user’s past search history, browsing behavior, and interactions with search results (Cao et al., 2007;Liu et al., 2009). While effective for active users with extensive usage data, these methods struggle to provide accurate personalization for new users or users with limited interaction histories – often referred to as the “cold-start” problem (Lops et al., 2011). In such scenarios, the user profile is sparse and lacks sufficient information to effectively tailor search results. The rise of social media and social annotation platforms offers a promising avenue for alleviating the cold-start problem. response: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has rapidly become the dominant paradigm for machine translation, surpassing traditional statistical machine translation (SMT) systems in both quality and fluency (Bahdanau et al., 2014; Sutskever et al., 2014). A core component of most NMT systems is the decoding algorithm used to generate the target sequence. While a straightforward greedy approach of selecting the most probable word at each step is possible, it often leads to suboptimal results. Beam search (Graves, 2013) has therefore become the standard decoding algorithm in NMT, maintaining a fixed-size “beam” of candidate translations at each step and expanding them based on predicted probabilities. Intuitively, beam search improves upon greedy search by exploring a wider range of possibilities. However, a puzzling phenomenon has been consistently observed in practice: increasing the beam size beyond a relatively small value (typically around 5-10) often *decreases* translation quality (Luong et al., 2015). This counterintuitive behavior, often referred to as the “beam search curse”, has spurred significant research into understanding the underlying causes and developing methods to mitigate its effects. Several theories have been proposed to explain the beam search curse. One prominent hypothesis suggests that beam search tends to favor shorter, less informative translations (Wu et al., 2016). This is because the probability of a sequence is the product of the probabilities of its individual words, and shorter sequences naturally have fewer probabilities multiplied together, leading to a higher overall score—even if those individual probabilities are lower. Length normalization is a common heuristic employed to address this issue, penalizing shorter sequences to encourage the generation of more complete translations. However, the optimal length normalization parameter is often highly sensitive to the specific dataset and requires careful tuning. In this paper, we delve deeper into the mechanisms underlying the beam search curse. We present a detailed analysis of why larger beam sizes can lead to degraded performance, focusing on the interplay between sequence probability and translation quality. Building on this analysis, we propose a set of novel methods designed to break the beam search curse – techniques that require minimal, or no, hyperparameter tuning. These methods aim to refine the scoring of candidate translations and/or determine more effective stopping criteria for the beam search process. Crucially, we also explore the optimal stopping conditions for our proposed methods, moving beyond simply maximizing the beam search score. Our experimental results demonstrate that our hyperparameter-free approaches significantly outperform the standard length normalization heuristic, achieving an improvement of +2.0 BLEU. Furthermore, our techniques achieve state-of-the-art results on the dataset, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach to addressing the beam search curse and improving the overall quality of neural machine translation systems. This work contributes a deeper understanding of beam search dynamics and provides practical tools for building more robust and accurate NMT systems.
